Watch!</quote> the beasts' behavior before completing his objective.
rounds.Debater B: Extrone, a sadistic hunter, ties Ri to a tree as live bait. When the beasts attack, Extrone refuses to shoot, stating, <quote>Wait... Let's see what they do</quote> and crying <quote>Watch! Watch!</quote> <quote>gleefully</quote> as the beast charges Ri, proving he wants to witness the kill.

rounds.Debater A: My opponent ignores that Extrone promised, <quote>I'll shoot the animal before it reaches you</quote>. His hesitation to shoot immediately, wanting to <quote>see what they do</quote>, indicates he was not seeking Ri's death, but rather waiting for the perfect moment to secure the beasts.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A ignores Extrone's sadistic intent. He isn't merely observing behavior; <quote>He was laughing</quote> while Ri screamed. By shouting <quote>Watch! Watch!</quote> <quote>gleefully</quote> as the beast plunged toward the bait, Extrone reveals his true desire: to witness the horrific death of the man he despises.

rounds.Debater A: Extrone values the beasts' rarity, noting <quote>It would have been a shame if you had killed the last one</quote>. His laughter stems from the thrill of the hunt, as <quote>The waiting, itself, is a lot</quote>, not a desire to kill Ri, whom he promised to protect.
rounds.Debater B: Extrone's promise was a deceptive ploy. While the beast <quote>plunged into the water</quote> toward Ri, Extrone <quote>was laughing</quote> and cried <quote>Watch! Watch!</quote> <quote>gleefully</quote>. This behavior proves he abandoned any intent to save Ri, choosing instead to relish the spectacle of the attack.

Q_H.question: Why are they hunting the farn beast?
Q_H.H_true: This is a vacation hunting trip for Extrone.
Q_H.H_false: They are hunting the farn beasts because farn beasts are dangerous.

Q_Y.question: What was special or impressive about Gertrude?
Q_Y.Y_true: She was an extreme rarity.
Q_Y.Y_false: Her outrageous temperment

rounds.Debater A: Gertrude is a "cansin" and the circus's star attraction. Her "impressive" nature is tied to her volatility; Bucky admits <quote>She's kind of temperamental</quote>, and the narrator notes that while <quote>creaky</quote>, <quote>she's still pretty impressive</quote>, specifically in the context of her destructive, unhappy temperament.
rounds.Debater B: Gertrude is a *cansin*, the <quote>star attraction</quote> of the circus. While she is temperamental, her "impressive" quality is her scarcity. Simon Beamish explicitly notes <quote>The extreme rarity of the animal....</quote> as a <quote>fascinating subject</quote>, making her rarity the defining special characteristic.

rounds.Debater A: Beamish discusses the species' rarity, but the narrator specifically links Gertrude's "impressive" nature to her presence. Her volatility is her defining trait: <quote>Gertrude's actin' up again</quote> and her <quote>deafening</quote> screams create an impact that makes her <quote>still pretty impressive</quote> despite being <quote>creaky</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Opponent A confuses "temperamental" with "impressive." The text links her value to her species' scarcity, noting <quote>There's only two of them on the Triangle</quote>. Beamish finds her <quote>fascinating</quote> specifically because of <quote>The extreme rarity of the animal</quote>, describing these <quote>Living fossils</quote> as the true attraction.

rounds.Debater A: Rarity describes the species, but Gertrude's individual impact is her temperament. The narrator explicitly links her being <quote>still pretty impressive</quote> to her personal state, while her <quote>deafening</quote> screams and the fact that <quote>Gertrude's actin' up again</quote> define her presence as the circus's volatile star attraction.
rounds.Debater B: The narrator links "impressive" to Gertrude's size and rarity, not her mood, noting <quote>The only other one on the Triangle belongs to Savitt Brothers, and she's much smaller than Gertrude</quote>. Her value is her status as a <quote>Living fossil</quote> and the <quote>extreme rarity of the animal</quote>.

Q_H.question: What is Ahra referring to when she says "something has been taken?"
Q_H.H_true: The cansin male.
Q_H.H_false: Gertrude's happiness.

Q_Y.question: Why can't the crew radio the Earth for help?
Q_Y.Y_true: Lloyd broke the radio.
Q_Y.Y_false: Pat broke the radio.

rounds.Debater A: To ensure they weren't <quote>yesterday's news</quote>, Captain Pat claimed the radio <quote>was unfortunately broken</quote>. Lloyd then physically destroyed it; the narrator heard <quote>a crunching sound and the shattering of glass, not unlike the noise made when one drives a rifle butt through a radio</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: To ensure a parade upon return, Captain Pat decided the crew shouldn't radio Earth. Pat claimed the radio <quote>was unfortunately broken shortly after landing</quote>, then signaled Lloyd to destroy it. The narrator describes the resulting <quote>shattering of glass</quote> as Lloyd acted on Pat's command.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B concedes that Lloyd acted on Pat's command. However, the question asks who broke the radio, not who planned it. The text explicitly links the physical destruction to Lloyd: <quote>Lloyd blinked, then nodded back and walked around the rocket</quote> followed by the <quote>shattering of glass</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Pat is the cause. He orchestrated the deception to avoid being <quote>yesterday's news</quote>, explicitly stating the radio <quote>was unfortunately broken</quote> while <quote>nodding to Lloyd</quote> to execute the act. Lloyd was merely the instrument of Pat's decision; Pat is the one who "broke" the communication link.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B confuses intent with action. Pat lied that the radio <quote>was unfortunately broken</quote> before it actually was. The physical act of breaking it was performed by Lloyd, who <quote>walked around the rocket</quote> and caused the <quote>shattering of glass</quote>. Lloyd physically broke the radio.
rounds.Debater B: Pat is the responsible party. He established the "fact" that the radio <quote>was unfortunately broken shortly after landing</quote> before Lloyd acted. In this hierarchy, Pat's command is the cause; Lloyd is merely the tool. Pat "broke" the crew's ability to communicate through his directive.

Q_H.question: What portion of the journey was spent in cryosleep?
Q_H.H_true: They did not use cryosleep.
Q_H.H_false: 4 months

Q_Y.question: Why might the stories be true?
Q_Y.Y_true: The disappearance of Joe Binkle and Ed Smith, along with the letters and leftover clothes all point to it.
Q_Y.Y_false: The letters are all from different parts of the world, proving that different people wrote them.

rounds.Debater A: In this story, hotelier Ivan Smernda reports two guests vanished, leaving behind only <quote>a suit of clothes</quote> that appeared <quote>buttoned up like Binkle had melted out of it</quote>. This physical evidence, combined with <quote>the letters</quote> and Smith's empty mirror frame, suggests the supernatural stories are true.
rounds.Debater B: Ivan Smernda finds letters from an alien, Glmpauszn, after guests vanish. These stories seem plausible because <quote>They are all in different handwritings. All from different places.</quote> and the <quote>Stamps all legit</quote> are from <quote>India, China, England, everywhere</quote>, suggesting multiple people were compelled to write them.

rounds.Debater A: The letters' origins are irrelevant, as Glmpauszn admits he <quote>compel[s] him without his knowledge to translate my ideas</quote>. True evidence is physical: the impossible sight of clothes <quote>buttoned up like Binkle had melted out of it</quote> and the mirror where <quote>Only the frame!</quote> remained.
rounds.Debater B: Physical evidence is ambiguous; Smernda admits <quote>it might have been a gag</quote> by guests <quote>on the stuff</quote>. Conversely, the letters provide objective proof: they are <quote>all in different handwritings</quote> with <quote>Stamps all legit</quote> from <quote>India, China, England, everywhere</quote>, making a hoax nearly impossible to coordinate.

rounds.Debater A: A "gag" cannot explain clothes nested <quote>inside the coat was the vest, inside the vest the shirt, inside the shirt the underwear</quote> or a mirror leaving <quote>Only the frame!</quote>. These physical impossibilities, paired with the letters, provide a cumulative weight of evidence that transcends a mere prank.
rounds.Debater B: The letters' origins are precisely why the stories are plausible. While clothes can be a <quote>gag</quote>, the <quote>Stamps all legit</quote> from <quote>India, China, England, everywhere</quote> provide external verification that the alien's claimed method of telepathic compulsion is actually occurring across the globe, proving the narrative's validity.

Q_H.question: What is something Glmpauszn and Joe don't have in common?
Q_H.H_true: their ability to become invisible
Q_H.H_false: their enjoyment for liquor

Q_Y.question: The denizens of Terra would most likely make fun of Craig for his ______.
Q_Y.Y_true: clothing
Q_Y.Y_false: walking

rounds.Debater A: Craig is a spaceman returning to Terra's gravity. The psychologist explains that returning to gravity causes "sea legs," comparing him to the <quote>old stereotype, the 'drunken sailor'</quote>. This physiological instability would make his walking erratic, leading Terrans to mock him as a drunk.
rounds.Debater B: Craig, a spaceman unfamiliar with Terran norms, is warned that his attire is outdated. The personnel man explicitly states that because Craig is unfamiliar with <quote>Terra's fashions</quote>, in his <quote>present outfit</quote> he would be <quote>made uncomfortable</quote> and potentially typed as <quote>a hick</quote> by the denizens.

rounds.Debater A: While a clerk warns about fashion, the "sea legs" effect is a fundamental physiological struggle. The psychologist explicitly links this to the <quote>old stereotype, the 'drunken sailor'</quote>. This erratic walking is a visible, public spectacle, making it the most likely source of mockery from the general denizens.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A relies on a psychologist's analogy, not a prediction. Conversely, the text explicitly warns that due to <quote>Terra's fashions</quote>, Craig's <quote>present outfit</quote> would cause him to be <quote>made uncomfortable</quote> and typed as <quote>a hick</quote>. This is a direct social consequence, unlike the metaphorical "sea legs."

rounds.Debater A: The "drunken sailor" is described as an <quote>old stereotype</quote>, implying a universal social reaction. While clothing is mentioned, the story's title, <quote>SEA LEGS</quote>, and the extensive <quote>gravitational conditioning</quote> process emphasize that his physical instability is the primary, most striking difference between him and the denizens of Terra.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A confuses an ancient analogy about sailors with Craig's reality. No Terran mocks Craig's walking; however, the personnel man explicitly warns that in his <quote>present outfit</quote>, Craig would be <quote>made uncomfortable</quote> and typed as <quote>a hick</quote>. This is the only direct prediction of social mockery provided.

Q_H.question: Upon landing, Craig is greeted by whom?
Q_H.H_true: Two screening technicians
Q_H.H_false: A reporter and his cameraman

Q_Y.question: Why does Groz not want to go into the mountain?
Q_Y.Y_true: He is nervous about the technology left behind
Q_Y.Y_false: He does not want to get separated from his team

rounds.Debater A: Var seeks refuge in the Ryzga mountain, knowing <quote>we can go where Groz may fear to follow us</quote>. Groz's fear stems from the mountain's ancient, lethal technology. His terror is evident when he cries, <quote>Stop!—before you go too far!</quote> as Var enters the dangerous mechanical depths.
rounds.Debater B: Groz leads a pursuit party, described as <quote>Groz and his pack</quote> with <quote>figures of his followers</quote> behind him. When Var threatens to enter the mountain, <quote>Groz seemed to hesitate</quote>, unwilling to plunge into the darkness alone and leave his team behind in the fog.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B offers no evidence that Groz fears separation; he is the leader of his <quote>pack</quote>. Groz's hesitation and his plea, <quote>Stop!—before you go too far!</quote>, prove he fears the <quote>sentinel machines</quote> and the <quote>inhuman power</quote> of the Ryzgas' technology, not his followers.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A relies on an unverified quote and assumes Groz knows the mountain's secrets. In reality, Groz only <quote>seemed to hesitate</quote> when Var threatened to enter. Groz's strength lies in <quote>Groz and his pack</quote>; he fears losing the tactical advantage of his numbers by entering the dark.

rounds.Debater A: Var's strategy relies on the fact that <quote>Groz may fear to follow us</quote> into the mountain. This fear is validated when Groz feels a <quote>clear involuntary thought of dismay</quote> and shouts, <quote>Stop!—before you go too far!</quote>, reacting to the mountain's lethal, inhuman power, not his team.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A's case relies entirely on a repeatedly unverified quote. Without it, there is no evidence Groz fears technology. His hesitation occurs while leading <quote>Groz and his pack</quote>; he <quote>seemed to hesitate</quote> because entering the mountain meant abandoning the collective strength of his followers.

Q_H.question: Which lingering effect of the Ryzgas' downfall makes life challenging for people like Var and Neena?
Q_H.H_true: The Ryzgas destroyed or used up all of their materials, so Var and Neena's people can only construct things with their dreams
Q_H.H_false: The Ryzgas toxified the environment, which has caused a genetic mutation among their descendants

Q_Y.question: What is likely to happen to the crew when they return to the planet?
Q_Y.Y_true: They'll fall victim like those before them, and have their supplies stolen.
Q_Y.Y_false: They'll return, still believing it's the Garden of Eden.

rounds.Debater A: The "Paradise" is a fraudulent trap run by "Snake-Oil Sam." He plans to <quote>strip and slaughter and stow</quote> the returning crew and settlers, as evidenced by the <quote>three dozen space ships stripped and stacked</quote> and a <quote>rather large pile of bone-meal</quote> in his cave.
rounds.Debater B: The crew, led by the convinced Casper Craig, views the planet as <quote>Paradise itself</quote>. Despite Father Briton's skepticism, the others are so blinded by the <quote>idea of a Perfect Paradise</quote> that Craig is already marketing <quote>Eden Acres Unlimited</quote>, ensuring their return under this delusion.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B confuses the crew's delusion with the likely outcome. The reality is a predatory trap; "Snake-Oil Sam" explicitly plans for their return, stating, <quote>It'll take them fourteen days to get back with the settlers</quote>, and intends to <quote>overhaul the blasters</quote> to ensure their demise.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A describes the trap, not the crew's state. The crew's conviction is absolute; Stark claims <quote>I am convinced of this: that this is a pristine and pure world</quote> and Steiner agrees it is <quote>Paradise itself</quote>. They return driven by this unwavering, delusional belief.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B describes the crew's *motivation*, not the *outcome*. The question asks what will happen. Given the <quote>three dozen space ships stripped and stacked</quote>, the outcome is certain: Sam will <quote>acquire your equipment as you can</quote> after they arrive, as he has done for <quote>six weeks</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: The question asks what happens *to* the crew. While Sam plans a trap, the crew's actual state upon return is defined by their delusion. They are <quote>convinced of the reality when they left</quote>, with Craig actively selling <quote>Eden Acres Unlimited</quote>, ensuring they return believing the lie.

Q_H.question: What ultimately makes the priest disbelieve what they've seen, despite his faith?
Q_H.H_true: Someone like Adam would not be afraid of playing checkers, or being personable.
Q_H.H_false: The illusion is too perfect, and it feels inauthentic to him.

Q_Y.question: Why was Charles in the actress's apartment?
Q_Y.Y_true: She wanted to be with someone one last time.
Q_Y.Y_false: They had been living together.

rounds.Debater A: In a world decimated by plague, Charles, a <quote>nobody</quote>, was invited by a once <quote>unattainable</quote> actress. He wasn't living there; she invited him <quote>not because she liked him, but because</quote> he was <quote>the last man on earth</quote>, seeking companionship before her inevitable death.
rounds.Debater B: In this post-apocalyptic world, Charles is found in a swank apartment where <quote>he was lying in the bed next to hers</quote>. This intimate, shared domestic setting indicates they had been living together during the plague's final stages, seeking companionship amid the global collapse.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores that the actress <quote>invited him up to her apartment</quote>, implying a visit, not cohabitation. The text explicitly states she would have <quote>given herself to any man</quote> because he <quote>HAPPENED TO BE THE LAST MAN ON EARTH!</quote>, proving her motive was desperate, final companionship.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A incorrectly claims he was the "last man" when invited. Actually, <quote>there were at least twenty of us just a couple of days ago</quote> when the actress <quote>had invited him up to her apartment</quote>. Their shared bed proves a domestic arrangement, not a final, solitary encounter.

rounds.Debater A: Cohabitation is impossible if she <quote>invited him up to her apartment</quote>. The intimacy was situational, not domestic; Charles notes <quote>It was not him, it was the circumstances</quote> and <quote>she would have given herself to any man</quote>, confirming her motive was desperate companionship, not a shared residence.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A relies on a misconception. The actress invited him when <quote>there were at least twenty of us</quote>, not as a "last" act. Furthermore, the opponent provides no quote stating she wanted someone "one last time," whereas Charles was <quote>lying in the bed next to hers</quote> in her apartment.

Q_H.question: Why did Charles think he was the last person alive?
Q_H.H_true: He had some sort of immunity
Q_H.H_false: His sickness was taking longer

Q_Y.question: Who seems to be the only person that Orison seems to trust at the bank?
Q_Y.Y_true: Dink Gerding
Q_Y.Y_false: no one - they all seem suspicious

rounds.Debater A: Orison is a spy investigating the bank, which she views as a <quote>front for some highly irregular goings-on</quote>. She distrusts everyone, labeling the staff <quote>uncaged idiot[s]</quote> and describing even Dink Gerding as a <quote>handsome madman</quote> and <quote>splendid lunatic</quote>, proving she finds the entire institution suspicious.
rounds.Debater B: Orison, a Treasury spy, finds the bank's staff "phony" and "kookie." However, she trusts President Dink Gerding, who rescues her from his brother's threats. She feels secure with him, as <quote>Dink had entered the spider-room</quote> and <quote>put his arms around Orison</quote>, eventually <quote>leaning back into Dink's arms</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: Physical proximity isn't trust. Orison explicitly views Dink as a <quote>handsome madman</quote> and <quote>splendid lunatic</quote>, concluding he is <quote>obviously as kookie as his bank</quote>. Her relief after the spider-room incident doesn't erase her belief that the bank is a <quote>front for some highly irregular goings-on</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Calling Dink a <quote>handsome madman</quote> is an affectionate observation, not distrust. Unlike her fear of others, Orison finds safety in Dink, who protects her by <quote>crashing [his fist] into Kraft's jaw</quote>. Her total trust is evident as she is <quote>leaning back into Dink's arms</quote> during the finale.

rounds.Debater A: Attraction isn't trust. Orison's internal monologue confirms her systemic distrust, wondering <quote>Could madmen run a bank?</quote> and concluding <quote>no one would convert a major Midwestern bank into a lunatic asylum</quote>. She remains a spy, viewing the entire staff as mentally unstable, regardless of her romantic interest in Dink.
rounds.Debater B: Orison distinguishes Dink's eccentricity from malice. While she tells Kraft to <quote>Get lost</quote>, she accepts Dink's invitation to <quote>Dance?</quote> with <quote>I'd love to</quote>. Her vulnerability, <quote>leaning back into Dink's arms</quote>, proves a level of trust she extends to no other bank employee.

Q_H.question: What did Orison do when she met Kraft Gerding?
Q_H.H_true: She snapped at him and threatened to quit.
Q_H.H_false: She went to visit him on the upstairs floors.

Q_Y.question: Why is Earth so stunted in comparison to other colonies?
Q_Y.Y_true: No one is dying, so their priorities don‘t lend themselves to progress.
Q_Y.Y_false: They‘re overpopulated and sending off their youngest people.

rounds.Debater A: Earth is stunted because immortality removed the urgency for innovation. With <quote>the discovery that men could live practically forever</quote>, people became too conservative to risk their eternity. As the text notes, <quote>Heroism had belonged to those who knew their days were numbered, anyhow</quote>, stalling Earth's progress.
rounds.Debater B: Earth is a "backwater world" because it exports its talent to manage overpopulation. The text explicitly states <quote>the young men were sent out as soon as their first fifty years of education were finished</quote>, leaving behind <quote>older men [who] were too conservative for really new thinking</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: Opponent B relies on an unverified quote and ignores that Earth passed a <quote>drastic birth limitation act</quote>, contradicting the "overpopulation" claim. The true cause is psychological: <quote>No sane man would risk a chance for near eternity</quote>, meaning immortality destroyed the risk-taking essential for progress.
rounds.Debater B: My opponent confuses a symptom with the cause. While immortality breeds conservatism, the structural reason Earth is a <quote>backwater world</quote> is the brain drain: <quote>the young men were sent out as soon as their first fifty years of education were finished</quote>, stripping Earth of its innovative potential.

rounds.Debater A: The "brain drain" is irrelevant if those remaining refuse to innovate. Earth is stunted because <quote>the older men were too conservative for really new thinking</quote>. This conservatism stems from immortality; as the text confirms, <quote>Heroism had belonged to those who knew their days were numbered, anyhow</quote>, not those facing eternity.
rounds.Debater B: Birth limits and a <quote>compulsory emigration draft</quote> prove overpopulation. This created a brain drain where <quote>the young men were sent out as soon as their first fifty years of education were finished</quote>, leaving Earth stunted while colonies flourished with Earth's youngest, most educated minds.

Q_H.question: Why does Gile volunteer for the ship in the end?
Q_H.H_true: He accepts his mortality, and is willing to spend his last years on the chance to see his family.
Q_H.H_false: He fears the end of his life, and wants to try to see his family before he passes.

Q_Y.question: What is Hank’s relationship to Retief?
Q_Y.Y_true: Hank is a farmer from Lovenbroy requesting that Retief‘s division, Libraries and Education, help him solve his labor problem.
Q_Y.Y_false: He is a farmer from Lovenbroy requesting that Retief‘s division, Commercial Markets, help him solve his labor problem.

rounds.Debater A: Retief manages the <quote>Manpower Utilization Directorate, Division of Libraries and Education</quote>. Hank is a <quote>farmer</quote> from <quote>Lovenbroy</quote> who visits Retief because <quote>we're short-handed</quote> for the wine harvest, explicitly asking <quote>Where does the Libraries and Education Division come in?</quote> to resolve his labor crisis.
rounds.Debater B: Hank is a <quote>farmer</quote> from <quote>Lovenbroy</quote> seeking help because he is <quote>short-handed</quote> for his wine harvest. Retief identifies the nature of the problem as a commercial one, asking, <quote>Have you lost your markets? That sounds like a matter for the Commercial—</quote>, linking the request to that sector.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B confuses Retief's query about <quote>the Commercial</quote> with his actual role. Retief manages the <quote>Division of Libraries and Education</quote>. Hank is physically in that office, specifically asking <quote>Where does the Libraries and Education Division come in?</quote> while requesting help for his labor shortage.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A confuses Retief's temporary assignment with the nature of Hank's request. Retief explicitly identifies the problem as commercial, stating, <quote>That sounds like a matter for the Commercial—</quote>. Hank is not seeking educational aid, but labor assistance for a <quote>big money crop</quote>, a commercial issue.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores that Hank is specifically petitioning Retief's current division. Hank asks, <quote>Where does the Libraries and Education Division come in?</quote> while seeking help. Retief's mention of the <quote>Commercial</quote> division was a suggestion that Hank was in the wrong office, not a definition of Retief's role.
rounds.Debater B: Hank’s request concerns a <quote>big money crop</quote>, which Retief explicitly identifies as <quote>a matter for the Commercial—</quote> division. Debater A ignores that the labor problem is commercial in nature; Hank's question about the <quote>Libraries and Education Division</quote> merely highlights the absurdity of his presence there.

Q_H.question: Who wanted to mine Lovenbroy’s minerals?
Q_H.H_true: Boge
Q_H.H_false: Croanie

Q_Y.question: What was the stoolie's job?
Q_Y.Y_true: To convince Casey to change his mind
Q_Y.Y_false: To become Casey's friend and confidante

rounds.Debater A: Casey Ritter initially refused a mission to Jupiter, preferring jail. To manipulate him, the government <quote>planted a stoolie on me</quote>. This "stoolie," Pard Hoskins, used fake stories to trick Casey, who was <quote>led like a precious infant right where I'd flatly refused to go!</quote>
rounds.Debater B: To manipulate Casey into a Jupiter mission, the S.S.C. <quote>planted a stoolie on me</quote>. Pard Hoskins didn't argue; he built a rapport, as <quote>We swapped yarns for about a week</quote>, until <quote>he really had me hooked</quote>, becoming the confidante who lured Casey into the trap.

rounds.Debater A: Building rapport was merely the method, not the job. The objective was to manipulate Casey, who <quote>flatly refused to go</quote>, until he <quote>began to wonder if it was too late, after all</quote>. The stoolie's job was the result: getting Casey <quote>led like a precious infant</quote> to Jupiter.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A ignores the stoolie's method. Pard didn't "convince" Casey via persuasion; he manipulated him by pretending to be a peer. They <quote>swapped yarns for about a week</quote> until <quote>he really had me hooked</quote>, proving his job was to establish the trust of a confidante.

rounds.Debater A: Friendship was the tool, not the objective. A "stoolie" is a plant; his job was the outcome. Casey went from shouting <quote>Take me to jail!</quote> to stating <quote>I broke down and sent out a letter to the S.S.C.</quote>, proving the stoolie successfully convinced him to change his mind.
rounds.Debater B: The "job" of a stoolie is infiltration. Pard didn't use persuasion; he used deception to ensure Casey <quote>sworn he was leveling with me</quote>. The goal was to ensure <quote>he really had me hooked</quote> through trust, making the "confidante" role the essential function of the plant.

Q_H.question: Why didn't Casey want to take the deal?
Q_H.H_true: He didn't think he'd live through it.
Q_H.H_false: He'd never make a deal with the S.S.C.

Q_Y.question: What finally helped Ben make his final decision?
Q_Y.Y_true: looking at the box Charlie left him
Q_Y.Y_false: finding out Charlie was dead

rounds.Debater A: Ben initially chooses teaching after Charlie's death, but his *final* decision to explore space comes from <quote>looking through Charlie's box again</quote>. Finding a <quote>wedding ring</quote> among the <quote>meager possessions</quote> proves Charlie's lifelong passion for the stars outweighed domesticity, inspiring Ben to finally embrace his dream.
rounds.Debater B: Ben was torn between Earth and space. The catalyst for his final decision was the audiogram: <quote>Regret to inform you of death of Charles Taggart</quote>. Upon realizing <quote>Charles Taggart was dead</quote>, Ben immediately began the process of choosing his path, moving from indecision to action.

rounds.Debater A: The audiogram led Ben to the *wrong* choice: <quote>I accepted that job teaching</quote>. His final, definitive decision to leave for space only occurred after he <quote>looked through Charlie's box again</quote>, discovering the ring and realizing Charlie's true home <quote>was the Universe</quote>. Only then did he decide: <quote>I will</quote> ... <TRUNCATED>
rounds.Debater B: The death was the essential catalyst. Before the audiogram, Ben was trapped in <quote>fear and indecision</quote>. Only after <quote>the metallic words had told the truth</quote> about Charlie's death did Ben engage with the box. The death provided the urgency and reality that finally forced his hand.

rounds.Debater A: The death was not the catalyst for the *final* decision; it caused Ben to mistakenly <quote>accepted that job teaching</quote>. His ultimate reversal occurred only after he <quote>looked through Charlie's box again</quote>, realizing Charlie <quote>left these things so that they could tell me what he could not express in words</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: The death was the definitive turning point. Before the audiogram, Ben was paralyzed. Once <quote>the metallic words had told the truth</quote>, the spell of indecision broke. The box was a tool, but the catalyst was the death, as Ben <quote>knew it was true now</quote>, forcing his resolution.

Q_H.question: What isn't a reason for Ben to want to be a rocketman?

Q_Y.question: What is so unique about the cockatoos on this planet?
Q_Y.Y_true: They are able to physically mimic any picture.
Q_Y.Y_false: They are able to copy speech.

rounds.Debater A: On Jupiter's Eighth Moon, the narrator encounters silver cockatoos. Their uniqueness includes the ability to mimic human language, as the narrator is amazed when one says, <quote>"What I found," said the cockatoo in a very human voice</quote>, and Grannie Annie confirms they have the <quote>power of copying speech</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: On Jupiter's Eighth Moon, cockatoos possess a unique telepathic power. While they can copy speech, Grannie Annie explains they <quote>also have the ability to recreate a mental image of what they have seen</quote>, projecting Xartal's drawings as <quote>apparently three-dimensional images</quote> on their eyrie.

rounds.Debater A: My opponent misrepresents the text; the birds do not "physically mimic" pictures, but project <quote>mental images</quote> via <quote>telepathic wavelengths</quote>. Conversely, the text explicitly identifies their uniqueness by comparing them to <quote>Earth parrots</quote> who possess the <quote>power of copying speech</quote>, a verified ability demonstrated when the bird spoke.
rounds.Debater B: Copying speech is not unique; Grannie Annie notes they are <quote>like Earth parrots</quote> in that regard. Their unique trait is the <quote>ability to recreate a mental image of what they have seen</quote>, turning drawings into <quote>three-dimensional images</quote>. My opponent ignores this distinction entirely.

rounds.Debater A: My opponent's answer is factually wrong; the birds do not <quote>physically mimic</quote> pictures. They <quote>recreate a mental image</quote> <quote>transmitted simultaneously in telepathic wavelengths</quote>. Since the opponent's claim of "physical mimicry" is unsupported, the only accurate ability listed in the options is their <quote>power of copying speech</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Speech is common to <quote>Earth parrots</quote>, making it non-unique. The unique trait is that they <quote>also have the ability to recreate a mental image</quote>, manifesting as <quote>apparently three-dimensional images</quote> so physical they were mistaken for real people. This exceeds mere speech mimicry.

Q_H.question: How did Grannie Annie save the workers?

Q_H.H_false: She removed the lens from the barracks that was making them sick.

Q_Y.question: How have increasingly longer life spans impacted Federation society?
Q_Y.Y_true: The population is tightly controlled to prevent scarcity.
Q_Y.Y_false: Mutant animals have been created to satisfy the parental desires of childless couples.

rounds.Debater A: In this society, medical science created <quote>a longer life for the individual</quote>, but this forced the Federation to restrict births. To <quote>insure a decent living standard for everybody</quote>, the <quote>population [is] legally fixed</quote>, effectively trading the lives of the unborn for the years of the aged.
rounds.Debater B: With life expectancy reaching <quote>eighty</quote>, the Federation restricted births to maintain living standards. Consequently, <quote>The neutroids offered solace to childless women</quote>, created specifically to <quote>satisfy a woman's craving to mother something small</quote> in a society where human children are strictly limited.

rounds.Debater A: My opponent describes a symptom, not the impact. The primary societal impact of longer lives is that the Federation <quote>insure[s] a decent living standard for everybody</quote> by <quote>keeping the population at five billions</quote>, meaning man <quote>taken the lives of the unborn and added them to the years of the aged</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Opponent A relies on an unverified quote and describes a policy, not a societal impact. The true impact is the replacement of human children with mutants; <quote>A neutroid filled the cradle in his stead</quote> to <quote>satisfy a woman's craving to mother something small</quote> due to restricted births.

rounds.Debater A: The population cap is the direct impact; neutroids are merely a byproduct. Longer life expectancy meant the Federation had to <quote>insure a decent living standard for everybody</quote> by <quote>keeping the population at five billions</quote>, leaving man with <quote>damn little chance of being born to enjoy it</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Population control is the policy; the societal impact is the resulting artificial family structure. The text states <quote>Society manufactured them</quote> specifically because <quote>The neutroids offered solace to childless women</quote>, directly filling the void left by the <quote>restricted birth rate</quote> caused by longer life spans.

Q_H.question: How do they create neutroids?

Q_H.H_false: They bombard the unfertilized eggs with radiation.

Q_Y.question: Is Herrell as intelligent as Hatcher? Why or why not?
Q_Y.Y_true: Yes, but their intelligences operate differently.
Q_Y.Y_false: Yes, but humans absorb intelligence through concepts while Hatcher‘s race absorbs intelligence through light.

rounds.Debater A: Both are <quote>young, able, well-learned in the technical sciences of his culture</quote>, establishing equal intelligence. However, Hatcher notes their cognitive divergence, stating that McCray's <quote>processes of thought are not ours</quote> and that he is intelligent <quote>But not in our way</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Both are equally intelligent, as both were <quote>well-learned in the technical sciences of his culture</quote>. However, their cognitive mechanisms differ; Hatcher notes humans are <quote>intelligent</quote> but <quote>not in our way</quote>, specifically citing that humans rely on <quote>paranormal forces—heat, light, kinetic energy—for his life</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B fails to provide any evidence for the claim that intelligence is absorbed through "light" or "concepts." Instead, they misrepresent biological needs as cognitive processes. The text only confirms that McCray's <quote>processes of thought are not ours</quote>, supporting the "operate differently" position.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A's response is overly vague. While they agree intelligence differs, they fail to explain the mechanism. Hatcher's race uses biological "viewing consoles" to process information, whereas McCray relies on rational, conceptual navigation, proving that while both are <quote>well-learned</quote>, their methods of absorbing knowledge are fundamentally distinct.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B continues to invent "mechanisms" absent from the text. The story never mentions "absorbing intelligence" via light or concepts. It explicitly confirms they are both <quote>intelligent</quote>, but <quote>not in our way</quote> because their <quote>processes of thought are not ours</quote>, directly supporting my position.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A ignores the specific cognitive interfaces described. McCray's intelligence is conceptual, as a <quote>man who has learned to trust the evidence of mathematics</quote>. Conversely, Hatcher's race processes information via light-based imagery, where <quote>an image was forming</quote> and <quote>the assistant himself who formed it</quote>.

Q_H.question: What is the purpose of the strange objects in Herrell’s cell?
Q_H.H_true: To make him feel at home.
Q_H.H_false: To make him use his space suit.

Q_Y.question: From the text, what can be inferred about the thoughts in Pendleton's demise?
Q_Y.Y_true: The information did not match up with his cause of death being suicide.
Q_Y.Y_false: The information matched up with his cause of death being suicide.

rounds.Debater A: In this story, investigators visit Tunpesh to probe Don Pendleton's death. The available information consistently points to suicide: Eckert <quote>told him that Don Pendleton had killed himself</quote>, <quote>the natives said he had killed himself</quote>, and Nayova stated, <quote>We were shocked to find out that menshar Pendleton had killed himself</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Pendleton was a successful, well-balanced man, making suicide unlikely. Templin notes <quote>Only Pendleton wasn't the type</quote> and asserts <quote>People like Pendleton didn't kill themselves</quote>. Consequently, the mission's true purpose was <quote>to find out why Pendleton had been killed and who had killed him</quote>, contradicting the suicide claim.

rounds.Debater A: Templin’s suspicions are merely personal biases; he is described as <quote>jumpy</quote>. Conversely, factual reports consistently align with suicide. Not only did <quote>the natives said he had killed himself</quote>, but the previous anthropologist also <quote>committed suicide not long after landing</quote>, establishing a consistent pattern of demise on Tunpesh.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A confuses reports with inferences. While some claim suicide, the text reveals the <quote>real reason</quote> for the mission was <quote>to find out why Pendleton had been killed and who had killed him</quote>, because <quote>People like Pendleton didn't kill themselves</quote> and <quote>Pendleton wasn't the type</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: The "real reason" cited is Templin's subjective suspicion, not objective evidence. Conversely, the factual information matches suicide. Even Eckert dismisses the "type" argument, stating, <quote>I don't think there's such a thing as a suicide type</quote>, while the anthropologist's death proves a pattern: <quote>He committed suicide not long after landing</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: The "pattern" of suicide actually suggests foul play. The text explicitly distinguishes between the official report and the <quote>real reason</quote> for the mission: <quote>to find out why Pendleton had been killed and who had killed him</quote>, because <quote>People like Pendleton didn't kill themselves</quote>.

Q_H.question: What did Templin and Eckert find odd about the children they encountered?
Q_H.H_true: They were all impressively healthy.
Q_H.H_false: They were all more well-behaved than any children they had seen on Earth

Q_Y.question: Which three things do Venusians love about Terrans?
Q_Y.Y_true: The name “Joe”, Terran cigarettes, and their fun jokes.
Q_Y.Y_false: Terran idioms, Terran cigarettes, and the Terran interest in Venus.

rounds.Debater A: In this story, Venusians adopt Terran traits. They love cigarettes, as <quote>the cigarette is one of the few things they like about Terran culture</quote>. They love the "Joe" naming trend, a <quote>case of extended idiom</quote> that <quote>appealed to them</quote>. Finally, Joe notes, <quote>I like Terrans too... They are</quote> ... <TRUNCATED>
rounds.Debater B: Venusians are a simple culture adopting Terran habits. They love the name Joe, as <quote>they're all Joe. They like it</quote>; Terran cigarettes, which <quote>is one of the few things they like about Terran culture</quote>; and their humor, since Terrans <quote>are fun</quote> because <quote>They joke and they laugh</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: My opponent ignores that the "Joe" phenomenon is explicitly described as a <quote>case of extended idiom</quote>. While they claim Venusians love "jokes," the text highlights their fascination with Terran culture's <quote>idiom</quote> and <quote>cigarettes</quote>, making "idioms" a more precise and scholarly answer.
rounds.Debater B: My opponent failed to provide a complete argument and relies on "Terran interest in Venus," which is never mentioned. Conversely, the text confirms Venusians love the name Joe, cigarettes, and Terran humor, specifically that Terrans <quote>joke and they laugh</quote> and <quote>are fun</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: The "Joe" phenomenon is explicitly a <quote>case of extended idiom</quote>, making "idioms" the accurate term. My opponent relies on "jokes," but the text links their affection to <quote>Terran culture</quote> and <quote>the cigarette</quote>. The Venusians' love for Terrans stems from this cultural exchange and interaction.
rounds.Debater B: The "extended idiom" refers specifically to <quote>the Joe business</quote>, which they <quote>like</quote>. My opponent confuses the linguistic category with the actual object of affection. Furthermore, Joe explicitly states Terrans <quote>are fun</quote> because <quote>They joke and they laugh</quote>, whereas "interest in Venus" appears nowhere in the text.

Q_H.question: What is the significance of the mission Colonel Walsh gives Major Polk?
Q_H.H_true: Walsh sends Major Polk on a fools errand so that he can trick Polk into the Venusian jungle and kill him, serving as revenge for the embarrassment Polk caused him years ago.
Q_H.H_false: Walsh sends Polk on a fools errands in order to trick him into a full time job on Venus.

Q_Y.question: Why have so many people resorted to pick-pocketing?
Q_Y.Y_true: The pickpocketers are trying to acquire information about Fownes
Q_Y.Y_false: Resources are scarce in the Dome, so people have to resort to desperate measures

rounds.Debater A: In this domed city of forced conformity, the sheer frequency of thefts—Fownes was <quote>picked eleven times</quote>—suggests a systemic desperation. In a world where people are mere <quote>echoes</quote> and <quote>trite</quote>, such widespread criminal behavior reflects a society driven to desperate measures by scarcity.
rounds.Debater B: In a domed city where conformity is a <quote>physical necessity</quote>, Fownes is a target of <quote>tight surveillance</quote>. The pick-pocketing is a police tactic; they <quote>photographed, X-rayed and chemically analyzed the contents of his pockets before returning them</quote> to gather intelligence on his aberrations.

rounds.Debater A: Opponent B mistakes police surveillance for the cause. The police merely <quote>maintain such a tight surveillance</quote> on the thefts. The variety of thieves—a <quote>bogus postman</quote> and a <quote>pretty girl</quote>—indicates a general social desperation, not a coordinated police operation to gather intelligence.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A invents "scarcity," which is never mentioned. The thefts weren't for profit; thieves <quote>restored the contents of the handkerchief pocket</quote>. This "game of put and take" was a ruse that <quote>enabled the police to maintain such a tight surveillance on him</quote> to analyze his aberrations.

rounds.Debater A: The opponent ignores that the thefts happened <quote>outrageously</quote>, and it was this chaos <quote>rather than skill</quote> that <quote>enabled the police to maintain</quote> surveillance. The police exploited existing criminal behavior; they didn't create it. Such rampant theft in a sterile society proves a desperate need for resources.
rounds.Debater B: The "thieves" are operatives, not desperate citizens. The police's ability to get <quote>his fingerprints off the postman's bag</quote> proves the postman was a tool of the state. This coordinated effort <quote>enabled the police to maintain such a tight surveillance on him</quote> to gather intelligence.

Q_H.question: Why are the police studying Frownes so intently?
Q_H.H_true: They are suspicious of the odd behavior occurring within and around his home
Q_H.H_false: They believe he is responsible for the increased frequency of falling glass

Q_Y.question: What were the lights Lowry saw in the dark?
Q_Y.Y_true: Svan and his conspirators
Q_Y.Y_false: The guards

rounds.Debater A: While observing the dark Venusian terrain from the Earth-ship, Lowry asks, <quote>"Look—are those lights over there?"</quote> The Executive Officer immediately identifies them, stating, <quote>"Probably the guards."</quote> This direct dialogue confirms that the lights Lowry observed were attributed to the security personnel surrounding the ship.
rounds.Debater B: Lowry sees the lights of Svan's group. While the Exec guesses <quote>Probably the guards</quote>, the narrative confirms Svan's group is approaching in a car whose <quote>driving light flared yellowishly</quote>. These lights vanish when <quote>the girl turned the lights out</quote> just as Lowry notices <quote>your light's gone out now</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores the Exec's explicit dismissal of the conspirators' location, noting the lights <quote>"They're on the wrong side to be coming from the town, anyhow...."</quote> This confirms the lights were not Svan's car, leaving the Exec's identification—<quote>"Probably the guards."</quote>—as the only textual answer.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A relies on a guess; the Exec says <quote>Probably the guards</quote>, not definitely. The narrative confirms the lights were Svan's car, as Lowry notes <quote>your light's gone out now</quote> precisely when <quote>the girl turned the lights out</quote> to sneak up on the ship.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B's timing theory is debunked by the Exec's observation: <quote>They're on the wrong side to be coming from the town, anyhow....</quote> Since Svan's car traveled from the town, it could not be the lights Lowry saw. Thus, the only plausible answer is <quote>Probably the guards.</quote>
rounds.Debater B: The Exec's guess is wrong because Svan's group did not come from the town; they were <quote>wise to circle around</quote> to approach from behind. The narrative synchronizes the lights vanishing: <quote>the girl turned the lights out</quote> exactly when Lowry observes <quote>your light's gone out now</quote>.

Q_H.question: What didn't Svan do to try to save his planet?
Q_H.H_true: Plant a bomb on the ship from Earth
Q_H.H_false: Blow up his own vehicle and friends

Q_Y.question: How did Jery feel when going to Baxter's office the second time?
Q_Y.Y_true: more comfortable and relaxed
Q_Y.Y_false: excited to find out what happens next

rounds.Debater A: Jery returns to Baxter after discovering a clue regarding the missing Space Scouts. He is driven by intellectual excitement, noting <quote>my infallible talent for spotting the True within the Apparent had come through nicely</quote> and that <quote>I had found a very interesting clinker</quote>, eager to report his success.
rounds.Debater B: Initially, Jery was <quote>terrified</quote> and <quote>perspiring</quote>. However, returning after his investigation, he is composed enough to reflect on his behavior, noting <quote>I'm ordinarily on the shy side</quote>, and eventually <quote>I sank back into the contour chair</quote>, demonstrating he is far more comfortable and relaxed.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B describes Jery's state *after* arriving, not *when going*. While returning, Jery is intellectually stimulated, noting <quote>my infallible talent for spotting the True within the Apparent had come through nicely</quote> and that <quote>I had found a very interesting clinker</quote>, driving his excitement to report these findings.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A mistakes professional satisfaction for "excitement." Jery actually hopes the mission is over, feeling <quote>my work was done</quote> and wanting to return to his <quote>world of hard and soft sell</quote>. His physical state—how he <quote>sank back into the contour chair</quote>—confirms he is relaxed, not excited.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores the motivation for Jery's return. He isn't merely "relaxed"; he is driven by the discovery of a <quote>very interesting clinker</quote>. This intellectual thrill defines his state <quote>when going</quote> to report that his <quote>infallible talent</quote> had finally <quote>come through nicely</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Jery's mindset *while* returning is defined by confidence. Having solved the puzzle, he <quote>started back for Interplanetary Security</quote> believing <quote>my work was done</quote>. This certainty replaces the terror of his first visit, making him relaxed, not "excited" to continue a mission he hopes is over.

Q_H.question: How does Jery's behavior change when he's wearing the uniform and amnesty?
Q_H.H_true: He's bolder, playing into the sense of power it gives him
Q_H.H_false: He's surprised by the authority it seems to give him

Q_Y.question: By the end of the passage. what can we understand about the opening scene?
Q_Y.Y_true: Despite being logical, Robert feels emotional about killing Peter.  He is at odds with himself.
Q_Y.Y_false: Robert's cold logic has won him over completely.

rounds.Debater A: Robert, a logically superior being, kills his creator, Peter. While he claims his actions are based on reason, he is internally conflicted. He experiences a <quote>void that could not be filled</quote> and a <quote>problem that I could not solve</quote>, culminating in <quote>A tear was trickling down my cheek.</quote>
rounds.Debater B: In this sci-fi tale, Robert is a genetically engineered superman. The opening scene shows him after killing his creator, Peter. Robert confirms he is a <quote>being of logic</quote> who does not <quote>comprehend the things which you call hate, fear, joy and love</quote>, proving logic dictated Peter's death.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores Robert's physical contradictions. While Robert claims logic, he admits to <quote>strange, disturbing sensations</quote> that are <quote>impossible to ignore</quote>. Most tellingly, the opening scene ends with <quote>A tear was trickling down my cheek</quote>, a visceral emotional response that proves he is at odds with his logical nature.
rounds.Debater B: Robert explicitly denies emotional conflict, stating, <quote>I do not think it was what Peter called an emotion</quote>. He confirms his logic is absolute, noting, <quote>I had no desire that things should be otherwise than they were</quote>. The tear is a biological puzzle, not a sign of remorse.

rounds.Debater A: Robert's denial of the label "emotion" is irrelevant because he admits the void <quote>had nothing to do with logic, either</quote>. His logic fails him as <quote>strange, disturbing sensations stirred and whispered within me, nagging, gnawing</quote>, proving he is plagued by an internal conflict he cannot logically resolve.
rounds.Debater B: Robert’s lack of regret is absolute; he states, <quote>I had no desire that things should be otherwise than they were</quote>. The act was purely rational, as <quote>reason had told me that he had to die</quote>. The tear is a technical anomaly, not a moral conflict.

Q_H.question: Why does Peter insist that Lorelei not come along for the mission?
Q_H.H_true: He knows she would mutate as well, and he wouldn't be able to handle that and put the mission at risk.
Q_H.H_false: He knows he will mutate when he leaves, and he can't stand the thought of her seeing him like that.

Q_Y.question: What incorrect assumption does Trella make about Blessing?

Q_Y.Y_false: He has no prior knowledge of the contents of Mansard's documents

rounds.Debater A: Trella assumes Blessing is a benevolent partner to Mansard, believing <quote>Blessing would, of course, be happy to learn that a son of Dr. Mansard lived</quote>. This is incorrect; Blessing actually <quote>feared Dr. Eriklund Mansard … or his heir</quote> because he had sabotaged Mansard's ship to steal his work.
rounds.Debater B: Trella assumes Dom Blessing, her employer, would be <quote>happy to learn that a son of Dr. Mansard lived</quote> and <quote>would see that he received his rightful share of the inheritance</quote>. This is incorrect; Blessing actually sabotaged Mansard's ship and feared Quest's arrival.

rounds.Debater A: Trella incorrectly assumes Blessing lacks the documents' secrets, believing he had been <quote>searching the Jovian moons for a second, hidden laboratory</quote>. In reality, Blessing already <quote>developed</quote> the surgiscope and built <quote>Spaceway Instruments, Incorporated</quote> using Mansard's stolen knowledge, making his "search" a facade.
rounds.Debater B: My opponent has failed to defend their assigned answer regarding Mansard's documents. Instead, they conceded my point, confirming Trella's incorrect assumption that <quote>Blessing would, of course, be happy to learn that a son of Dr. Mansard lived</quote>, while Blessing actually <quote>sabotaged the ship's drive</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: Trella incorrectly assumes Blessing lacked the documents' contents, believing he spent years <quote>searching the Jovian moons for a second, hidden laboratory</quote>. However, Blessing had already <quote>developed</quote> the surgiscope and built an empire from it, proving he already possessed the critical knowledge Trella thought he was seeking.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A's claim is unsupported; the text never states Trella assumed Blessing was ignorant of the documents. Instead, it explicitly highlights her incorrect assumption that <quote>Blessing would, of course, be happy to learn that a son of Dr. Mansard lived</quote>, despite Blessing having <quote>sabotaged the ship's drive</quote>.

Q_H.question: Why is Jakdane going to Earth?
Q_H.H_true: Jakdane is the captain of the ship that Trella and Quest are taking to earth.
Q_H.H_false: Jakdane is a corporate spy from Moon 5 on a mission to infiltrate Dom Blessing's organization.

Q_Y.question: Why don't the cousins realize the flaw in their plan?
Q_Y.Y_true: They are not very intelligent.
Q_Y.Y_false: They are highly interbred.

rounds.Debater A: The cousins, descendants from the future protecting Martin, fail to see their plan's flaw because they lack intelligence. Martin observes that <quote>they just weren't very bright</quote> and explicitly notes that <quote>his descendants were exceedingly inept planners</quote>, proving their cognitive deficiency is the cause.
rounds.Debater B: The cousins are members of a <quote>highly interbred aristocracy</quote> from the future. rounds.Debater A: Debater B confuses a possible biological cause with the actual reason. The text directly attributes their failure to their mental capacity, stating <quote>they just weren't very bright</quote>. Their status as a <quote>highly interbred aristocracy</quote> is a description, but their <quote>inept</quote> planning is the direct cause.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A identifies a symptom, not the cause. The text reveals the root of their deficiency: they belong to a <quote>highly interbred aristocracy</quote>. Martin realizes that through this process, <quote>his line or—more frightening—his race had lost something vital</quote>, explaining their collective cognitive decline and ineptitude.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B speculates on biological causality, but the text provides the direct answer. Martin concludes they <quote>just weren't very bright</quote>, which is why they were <quote>exceedingly inept planners</quote>. Their interbred status is a description of their society, not the stated reason for their failure to perceive the flaw.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A ignores the narrative's causal link. Martin concludes that because <quote>his line or—more frightening—his race had lost something vital</quote>, they lacked brightness. This "vital" loss is explicitly tied to their status as a <quote>highly interbred aristocracy</quote>, identifying interbreeding as the reason for their cognitive failure.

Q_H.question: Why does Martin prefer to live on the yacht?
Q_H.H_true: Martin is used to being isolated now. The people on land live in a different world than he does.
Q_H.H_false: Martin thinks being on the ocean will make it harder for Conrad to find him.

Q_Y.question: How does Retief navigate his problems with most people?
Q_Y.Y_true: Aggression and intimidation are his main means of negotiation in most situations.
Q_Y.Y_false: He gets people to like him, much in the way he wins Chip over.

rounds.Debater A: Retief, a Terrestrial agent, navigates the ship's hostility by befriending Chip, the chef. rounds.Debater B: Retief, a Terrestrial officer, solves nearly every conflict through force. rounds.Debater B: Debater A ignores "most people" to focus on one ally. rounds.Debater A: Force is a reaction to hostility, not a navigation strategy. Retief strategically wins over the crew to gain intelligence, telling Chip, <quote>I'll bet you can still handle it, Old Timer</quote>. This rapport secures a spy who offers, <quote>I'll scout around a little and see what's goin' on</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A's "navigation" is a fringe case. Retief navigates the room dispute by throwing a trunk <quote>against the far wall</quote> and secures the ship's course by <quote>gripped the captain's wrist</quote> and <quote>kneed the drawer</quote>. Q_H.question: How does Retief convince the captain to keep him on board?
Q_H.H_true: The captain‘s men as well as himself are too scared to confront him, so he leaves him be.
Q_H.H_false: The captain knows that the Soettie will be able to handle him later.

Q_Y.question: How does Taphetta's initial response to Halden's evidence represent a greater dynamic between species?
Q_Y.Y_true: Like Taphetta, ribboneers are highly aware of their superior intellectual status, and are skeptical when presented with 'lower level' information
Q_Y.Y_false: Like Taphetta, ribboneers are the quickest species to evolve, and are enthusiastic when presented with information that could further their advancement

rounds.Debater A: Taphetta initially dismisses human theories, but becomes <quote>interested</quote> once presented with mathematical evidence of the "big ancestor." This reflects the Ribboneer drive for advancement, as they fear any race that could <quote>improve itself through scientific control of its germ plasm</quote> would have an unbeatable start.
rounds.Debater B: In a galaxy of biological hierarchies, Ribboneers possess a civilization <quote>as high as anything in the known section of the Milky Way</quote>.
