story_title: The Haunted Fountain: A Judy Bolton Mystery

Q_Y.question: Of the three, who seems to keep holding secrets in more than the others?
Q_Y.Y_true: Lorraine
Q_Y.Y_false: Judy

rounds.Debater A: In this story of three friends, Lorraine is the most secretive. While Judy shares her past, Lorraine is evasive about her husband, as <quote>Lois and Judy both questioned Lorraine, but that was all she would say</quote>, and she <quote>ducked her head</quote> to hide from a passing driver.
rounds.Debater B: Judy’s history is defined by secrecy. She admits <quote>keeping that promise not to talk about the dam was a great big mistake</quote> and kept the fountain's mystery hidden so long that Lois exclaimed, <quote>I didn’t dream you’d kept anything that exciting a secret</quote>, proving a pattern of withholding information.

rounds.Debater A: Judy is currently disclosing her past, whereas Lorraine actively hides the present. Judy notes, <quote>You’re the one who seems to know the answers, but you’re not telling</quote>. Lorraine remains <quote>evasive</quote> about her husband and the estate, proving she holds more current secrets than the open and honest Judy.
rounds.Debater B: Lorraine’s current evasiveness is momentary, but Judy’s secrecy is habitual. Judy kept the fountain a secret for years, and her past includes a <quote>great big mistake</quote> in <quote>keeping that promise not to talk about the dam</quote>, demonstrating a long-term pattern of withholding critical information.

rounds.Debater A: Judy’s past "secrets" were promises or memories she now openly shares. Lorraine’s secrecy is active and suspicious; she <quote>ducked her head</quote> in fear, and Judy notes that <quote>hiding your face back there gave you away</quote>. Lorraine remains <quote>evasive</quote>, concealing current, potentially dangerous information.
rounds.Debater B: The question asks who *keeps* holding secrets. While Lorraine is currently evasive, Judy’s life is defined by them. She admits, <quote>I do have problems, and there are plenty of mysteries I can’t solve</quote> and notes her grandparents <quote>left me a lot of unsolved mysteries along with this house.</quote>

Q_H.question: Why did Judy start crying in the attic of her grandparents home?
Q_H.H_true: She was lonely with no friends.
Q_H.H_false: She was sad that her parents wouldn't let her come on their vacation.

Q_Y.question: Why are Arvid 6 and Tendal 13 attempting to steal Reggie?
Q_Y.Y_true: Kanad was accidentally sent transformed to Reggie's body by mistake in the Ultroom.
Q_Y.Y_false: They need infants for experiments they are conducting in the Ultroom.

rounds.Debater A: Arvid 6 and Tendal 13 are recovering the "life germ" of Kanad, the galactic head, after Arvid 6 accidentally sent him back 6,000 years. They must <quote>rescue the life germ of Kanad out of each era he'd be born in</quote> to <quote>correct a mistake Arvid 6 made!</quote>
rounds.Debater B: Arvid 6 and Tendal 13 are agents of the Ultroom tasked to <quote>rescue the life germ of Kanad out of each era he'd be born in</quote>. They target infants like Reggie to facilitate this scientific <quote>transplanted to a younger body</quote> procedure, which constitutes their Ultroom operations.

rounds.Debater A: My opponent incorrectly suggests general "experiments." The text clarifies they are on a specific rescue mission <quote>to bring Kanad back, to correct a mistake Arvid 6 made!</quote> after <quote>sending him back beyond his original birth date</quote>, requiring them to retrieve his life germ from Reggie's body.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A fails to address the specific answer. The goal is not a "transformation" but to <quote>rescue the life germ of Kanad out of each era he'd be born in</quote> for the purpose of being <quote>transplanted to a younger body</quote>, a clinical Ultroom experiment.

rounds.Debater A: Opponent's "experiment" theory is baseless. The text explicitly labels this an <quote>Ultroom error</quote> and a <quote>mistake Arvid 6 made!</quote> by <quote>sending him back beyond his original birth date</quote>. They are not conducting experiments; they are retrieving Kanad, who was accidentally displaced across eras.
rounds.Debater B: The "rescue" is an Ultroom procedure to be <quote>transplanted to a younger body</quote>. Opponent's "transformation" claim is false; they must <quote>rescue the life germ of Kanad out of each era he'd be born in</quote>. This systematic extraction from infants is the very experiment the Ultroom conducts.

Q_H.question: What was Arvid 6's mistake?
Q_H.H_true: Arvid 6 transferred Kanad back in time 6000 years.
Q_H.H_false: Arvid 6 dropped the baby when the dog started barking at him.

Q_Y.question: Why did Moynihan shoot Stanley?
Q_Y.Y_true: Stanley tried to poison him.
Q_Y.Y_false: Stanley was protecting Albert Peet.

rounds.Debater A: Jaro Moynahan shot Stanley because Stanley acted as the hired protector for Albert Peet, a corrupt tycoon. Stanley was the <quote>baby-faced gunman your boss had in his office</quote>, and Peet explicitly stated <quote>I had a job for him</quote>, positioning Stanley as Peet's violent enforcer.
rounds.Debater B: Moynahan, a professional soldier, shot Stanley in self-defense when Stanley's <quote>hands began to creep upward</quote> to attack. Moynahan subsequently seized Stanley's <quote>two poisoned needle guns</quote>, later explaining to Joan Webb that Stanley <quote>took a pot shot at me with that poisoned dart gun</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: While Debater B describes the immediate skirmish, they ignore Stanley's fundamental role. Moynahan shot him because Stanley was Peet's hired muscle, the <quote>baby-faced gunman your boss had in his office</quote>. Peet's admission, <quote>I had a job for him</quote>, confirms Stanley's purpose was protecting Peet's interests.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A confuses Stanley's employment with the cause of the shooting. Moynahan shot Stanley because Stanley attempted to use <quote>poisoned needle guns</quote> when his <quote>hands began to creep upward</quote>. Moynahan explicitly confirms it was self-defense because Stanley <quote>took a pot shot at me with that poisoned dart gun</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B focuses on the *mechanism* of the fight, not the *motive*. Stanley only attacked because he was Peet's <quote>baby-faced gunman</quote> tasked with a <quote>job for him</quote>. His aggression was a direct function of his role protecting Peet's interests against Moynahan's interference.
rounds.Debater B: Stanley's employment is irrelevant to the trigger. Moynihan shot him because of a specific lethal threat: Stanley's <quote>hands began to creep upward</quote> to use <quote>poisoned needle guns</quote>. Moynihan confirms the motive was self-defense because Stanley <quote>took a pot shot at me with that poisoned dart gun</quote>.

Q_H.question: How did the Mercurians adjust to the heat?
Q_H.H_true: They mostly lived under the ground.
Q_H.H_false: Their yellow eyes filtered the sun‘s rays.

Q_Y.question: Why did Davies attach himself to Infield outside of Infield & Morgan?
Q_Y.Y_true: He was afraid of heights and falling over, so he had affixed himself to Infield in order to calm his fear.
Q_Y.Y_false: He was attempting to catch Infield after he ran away from the fraternal club for the Cured.

rounds.Debater A: In a world of mechanical "Cures" for phobias, Davies uses a <quote>Model Acrophobe 101-X</quote> safety belt. Terrified of falling, Davies accidentally attaches to Infield via magnetic darts. When urged to release, Davies groans, <quote>I'm scared!</quote>, confirming his actions were driven by his fear as an <quote>acrophobe</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: In this dystopian world, the "Cured" form a tight-knit society. Davies, using his safety belt, attached himself to Infield to prevent his escape from the influence of the Cured, as seen when Price later insists, <quote>We've got to stop him for good</quote> and <quote>go after him.</quote>

rounds.Debater A: Debater B uses quotes from the story's end to explain an earlier event. When Davies attached to Infield, he was <quote>quivering in the center of a web</quote> and admitted, <quote>I'm scared!</quote> His <quote>Model Acrophobe 101-X</quote> belt proves his attachment was a panic response to his fear of falling.
rounds.Debater B: Opponent A ignores the pursuit. After Infield leaves the club, Price commands, <quote>We've got to stop him for good. We've got to go after him.</quote> Davies, as part of this group, pursues Infield to prevent his escape, making the attachment a calculated attempt to capture a defector.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B confuses two separate events. The attachment occurred when Infield first <quote>stepped into the main stream of human traffic</quote>, long before Price's later command to pursue him. Davies' panic—<quote>I'm scared!</quote>—and his <quote>Model Acrophobe 101-X</quote> belt prove this was a phobia-driven accident, not a calculated capture.
rounds.Debater B: The "web" of cables <quote>stuck secure to the walls</quote> and Infield demonstrates a systemic attempt to snare individuals. This aligns with the Cured's mission to <quote>stop him for good</quote>, proving the attachment was not a random accident, but a method of capturing those who defy them.

Q_H.question: What is normal about the Incompletes?
Q_H.H_true: They still live with a specific fear
Q_H.H_false: They are only partially cured

Q_Y.question: Which of these is true about the Red Mask?
Q_Y.Y_true: He is entirely harmless and it just looks like he's trouble
Q_Y.Y_false: He does not hesitate to use physical violence

rounds.Debater A: The Red Mask was a "Nilly," a professional scapegoat hired to prevent colonist infighting. While he appeared dangerous, he was <quote>entirely harmless</quote> in reality. Critten admits, <quote>I was a liar</quote> and <quote>Lucky nobody got hurt during any of it</quote>, including the staged assault he <quote>did not</quote> commit.
rounds.Debater B: In this story, the Red Mask terrorizes the *Weblor II*. He is linked to a <quote>severe beating</quote> that killed Raymond Palugger. Even after the twist, he admits he <quote>got a stunner and robbed along the corridor</quote>, proving he uses physical force to achieve his goals.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B relies on falsehoods. The "severe beating" was a ruse; Critten reveals <quote>Raymond Palugger died... from his illness on the operating table</quote>. Furthermore, Critten explicitly confirms, <quote>Lucky nobody got hurt during any of it</quote>, proving he never used violence, only deception and non-harmful stunners.
rounds.Debater B: My opponent ignores that Red Mask used a weapon to commit crimes. He admits, <quote>I got a stunner and robbed along the corridor</quote>, and specifically <quote>put occupants to sleep as he went</quote> using that stunner. Using a weapon to incapacitate others is physical violence, regardless of the ultimate intent.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B conflates incapacitation with violence. The narrative's climax reveals the Red Mask's role was a fabrication; Critten explicitly confirms, <quote>Lucky nobody got hurt during any of it</quote>. Since he admits <quote>I was a liar</quote>, the "violence" was a staged illusion, making him entirely harmless.
rounds.Debater B: My opponent confuses "injury" with "violence." Forcibly incapacitating people with a weapon is physical violence. Critten admits he <quote>got a stunner and robbed along the corridor</quote>, and specifically <quote>put occupants to sleep as he went</quote>. Using a weapon to overpower others is an act of physical violence.

Q_H.question: What is the significance of the story's title?
Q_H.H_true: There is a man on board hired specifically to act as the weight to keep the others balanced
Q_H.H_false: It hints at the importance of the balance of weight on the ship for successful mission

Q_Y.question: What would have happened if Allen's blaster had not run out of charge?
Q_Y.Y_true: He would still have hit the switch, ending the story the same way.
Q_Y.Y_false: He would have been able to shoot the switch from where he stood instead of having to make a run for it.

rounds.Debater A: Alan discovered <quote>The blaster static blanks out radio transmission from the computer</quote>, neutralizing the robots. Because <quote>his blaster quit</quote> just before the door, he was forced to <quote>race painfully for the door</quote> and dive for the switch instead of disabling the robot from a distance.
rounds.Debater B: Alan's blaster was a <quote>pop gun</quote> that <quote>wouldn't even singe a robot</quote>; its only use was creating <quote>blaster static</quote> to confuse them. Since he had to physically hit the <quote>red-clad safety switch</quote> to disable the computer, having more charge wouldn't change the necessary outcome.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores the *process*. Without the blaster's static, Alan was vulnerable, forced to <quote>race painfully for the door</quote> and <quote>fumble with the lock release</quote> while being shot at. More charge would have allowed him to maintain the robots' confusion from a distance.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A falsely claims Alan could "disable" robots from a distance. The text explicitly states his <quote>pop gun wouldn't even singe a robot</quote>. Since the blaster only provides <quote>blaster static</quote> for <quote>a few seconds</quote>, he must still hit the <quote>red-clad safety switch</quote> to end the threat.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B conflates destroying robots with hitting a switch. While the blaster <quote>wouldn't even singe a robot</quote>, it could easily trigger the <quote>red-clad safety switch</quote> from afar. Because <quote>his blaster quit</quote>, he was forced to <quote>half-jump, half-fell towards it</quote> in a desperate, physical rush.
rounds.Debater B: The "process" is irrelevant to the outcome. Since static only blanks transmissions <quote>for a few seconds</quote>, Alan could never permanently disable robots from afar. He must reach the <quote>red-clad safety switch</quote> to stop the computer; thus, the story ends the same way regardless of charge.

Q_H.question: How does the darkness affect the robots' mobility?
Q_H.H_true: Their mobility is not affected, but it is harder for them to aim their blasters.
Q_H.H_false: Their tracking of animals is unimpeded, but they still have plans to contend with.

Q_Y.question: What is the Brightside?
Q_Y.Y_true: The Brightside is the side of Mercury that constantly faces the sun.
Q_Y.Y_false: The Brightside is the first passage to the core of Vulcan Crater on Venus.

rounds.Debater A: The story introduces the "Brightside" within the context of elite planetary exploration. It highlights Balmer, who <quote>mapped the first passage to the core of Vulcan Crater on Venus</quote>, establishing the precedent for the perilous "Brightside Crossing" attempts discussed by Baron and Claney.
rounds.Debater B: In this sci-fi story, characters attempt a perilous "Crossing" of Mercury. The text explicitly defines the Brightside: <quote>Mercury turns on its axis in the same time that it wheels around the Sun, which means that the Brightside is always facing in.</quote>

rounds.Debater A: The text links the "Brightside" to the legacy of explorers like Balmer. While the opponent focuses on geography, the narrative emphasizes the "Crossing." Balmer <quote>mapped the first passage to the core of Vulcan Crater on Venus</quote>, establishing the type of feat Baron seeks with the Brightside.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A fails to define the Brightside, instead citing a mission to Venus. The text explicitly separates these: Balmer mapped <quote>Vulcan Crater on Venus</quote>, but the <quote>Brightside of Mercury</quote> is defined as the side <quote>always facing in</quote> toward the Sun.

rounds.Debater A: The narrative intertwines the "Brightside" with the most prestigious feats of exploration. By highlighting Balmer, who <quote>mapped the first passage to the core of Vulcan Crater on Venus</quote>, the story establishes the Brightside as the ultimate frontier, mirroring the prestige of the Vulcan Crater achievement.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A continues to conflate two different planets. The text explicitly distinguishes <quote>Vulcan Crater on Venus</quote> from the <quote>Brightside of Mercury</quote>. The Brightside is not a "type of feat" but a specific location: the side of Mercury <quote>always facing in</quote> toward the Sun.

Q_H.question: What doesn't Baron think was a reason for their failure?
Q_H.H_true: the Major's experience
Q_H.H_false: poor mapping

Q_Y.question: What is the relationship between the Hairy people and the Furry people?
Q_Y.Y_true: The Furry people hunt the Hairy, because they were once enslaved by them.
Q_Y.Y_false: The Furry people have a disdain for the Hairy, and frequently attack them.

rounds.Debater A: On the hanging world of Lomihi, the Furry people are aggressors who <quote>raid the Hairy People</quote>. Their relationship is defined by violent hostility; for instance, when spotting a Hairy person, the <quote>warrior women shrieked their hatred</quote>, confirming a deep disdain and a pattern of frequent attacks.
rounds.Debater B: On the hanging world Lomihi, the Furry people <quote>raid the Hairy People</quote> to <quote>take them for slaves</quote>. This enmity stems from a historical reversal: <quote>The Hairy People were the rulers</quote> and <quote>the Furry Ones were their slaves</quote> before a revolt split the races.

rounds.Debater A: My opponent relies on an inferred causal link. While slavery existed, the text emphasizes active, visceral hatred. The <quote>warrior women shrieked their hatred</quote>, and the current relationship is one of aggression where they <quote>raid the Hairy People</quote>, fitting my description of disdain and frequent attacks.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A describes only the surface-level hostility. My answer provides the essential cause: <quote>The Hairy People were the rulers</quote> and <quote>the Furry Ones were their slaves</quote>. This historical enslavement explains why the Furry people now <quote>raid the Hairy People</quote> to <quote>take them for slaves</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: The relationship is defined by current actions, not ancient history. My opponent confuses origin with relationship. The Furry are <quote>bloodthirsty warrior women</quote> who <quote>raid the Hairy People</quote>. This active, violent hostility and <quote>hatred</quote> perfectly matches my answer, whereas "hunt" inaccurately describes these raids.
rounds.Debater B: The causal link is explicit, not inferred. The <quote>revolt that eventually split Lomihi into two warring races</quote> transformed the <quote>Furry Ones</quote> from <quote>slaves</quote> into aggressors who now <quote>raid the Hairy People</quote> to <quote>take them for slaves</quote>, mirroring their own former oppression.

Q_H.question: What is Rolf's new plan when he spots the rocket?
Q_H.H_true: He'll be able to distribute water to Mar's colonies, and get out with Tanner and the girl.
Q_H.H_false: He'll have a way out of the caverns at last, be able to escape.

Q_Y.question: How does the Dean feel about Caswell?
Q_Y.Y_true: The Dean views Caswell as a friend and co-conspirator.
Q_Y.Y_false: The Dean thinks Caswell is a stuck-up intellectual.

rounds.Debater A: The Dean views Caswell as a pretentious academic. He dismisses Caswell's Latin degrees as merely <quote>supposed to be signs of great learning</quote> and admits, <quote>I smiled condescendingly, knowing it would irritate him</quote>, treating Caswell's intellectualism as a barrier to the <quote>brass tacks</quote> of university funding.
rounds.Debater B: Initially tense, the Dean and Caswell become partners in a social experiment. The narrator explicitly states, <quote>We were friends now</quote>, and describes them <quote>talking in conspiratorial tones</quote> while designing a "deadly little organization" together, proving they evolved into friends and co-conspirators.

rounds.Debater A: The Dean's "friendship" is superficial; he still views Caswell through the lens of academic pretension. He attributes Caswell's behavior to being <quote>a man with a string of degrees after his name</quote>, confirming that he defines Caswell primarily by his intellectual status and the perceived arrogance accompanying it.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A ignores the story's progression. While initially tense, the Dean eventually calls him <quote>Perfect, Wilt, perfect!</quote>, using his first name. Their bond is cemented through their shared secret, as they <quote>got together and had lunch in a bar</quote> after their experiment succeeded.

rounds.Debater A: The Dean's perception remains rooted in academic stereotypes. Even as "friends," he views Caswell's behavior as a typical academic using success to <quote>rub my nose in the realization that I had been wrong</quote>, concluding that <quote>A man with a string of degrees after his name is just as</quote> ... <TRUNCATED>
rounds.Debater B: Debater A misinterprets the Dean's observation that a man with degrees is <quote>just as human as anyone else</quote>, which actually humanizes Caswell. Their bond is deep, not superficial; they spent hours <quote>conspiring</quote> to manipulate a town, eventually becoming <quote>friends</quote> who shared a secret, celebratory lunch.

Q_H.question: What is the relationship between Caswell and the protagonist?
Q_H.H_true: One is the other's boss
Q_H.H_false: They're coworkers

Q_Y.question: Which word best describe Wayne’s worst fear?
Q_Y.Y_true: Punk
Q_Y.Y_false: Gun

rounds.Debater A: In this dystopian world, youth must kill to prove their manhood. Wayne’s fear centers on the lethal instruments of this test; while examining his weapons, he finds the experience <quote>exciting and scary</quote>. The gun represents the violent threshold he ultimately fears he cannot cross.
rounds.Debater B: Wayne fears mediocrity and weakness. In a society where killing "undesirables" proves manhood, failing to execute his target means he <quote>punked out</quote>. His ultimate horror is realizing his parents <quote>had all punked out. Like him</quote>, confirming his worst fear: being a weak "punk" rather than a predator.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B confuses a label for failure with an object of fear. Wayne's actual fear is visceral and tied to the weapons; as he handles them, <quote>his mouth went dry</quote> and the experience was <quote>exciting and scary</quote>. The gun represents the lethal act he ultimately cannot perform.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A mistakes temporary nerves for a "worst fear." Wayne uses the gun without hesitation; his true failure is emotional. He despises his <quote>punkie origins</quote> and is devastated to realize he <quote>punked out</quote>, ultimately fearing he is just like the parents he loathed: <quote>They had all punked out. Like him.</quote>

rounds.Debater A: Debater B mistakes a social label for a fear. "Punk" is the result of his failure, not the source of his dread. His visceral terror is tied to the weapons; the blade's gleam was <quote>exciting and scary</quote> and made <quote>his mouth went dry</quote>, signaling his true fear.
rounds.Debater B: Wayne’s reaction to weapons is <quote>fearful exhilaration</quote>, not dread. His true horror is existential. He loathes his <quote>punkie origins</quote> and is devastated to discover he is identical to the parents he despised: <quote>They had all punked out. Like him.</quote> Being a "punk" is his ultimate failure and fear.

Q_H.question: Why doesn’t Wayne like his parents?
Q_H.H_true: He feels that they are soft and stupid, that they‘ve given up on what life has to offer.
Q_H.H_false: His parents want to keep him from breaking out, knowing that the horrors Wayne will face are too much for him.

Q_Y.question: Which is not a reason Ggaran might have asked a bowman to shoot a soldier in front of Crownwall?
Q_Y.Y_true: To punish the solider for his earlier misstep
Q_Y.Y_false: To demonstrate the use of traditional weapons in political situations

rounds.Debater A: Ggaran shot the soldier to illustrate the fate of <quote>civilians who violate this particular tradition</quote> of clearing streets. While the Viceroy notes guards must use <quote>pikes and bows and arrows</quote> for <quote>occasions of ceremony</quote>, there is no mention of demonstrating weapons for "political situations."
rounds.Debater B: Ggaran killed a soldier merely as a hypothetical demonstration for Crownwall, stating, <quote>Let us just suppose that that runner over there... is a civilian</quote>. He did so to show how they handle <quote>civilians who violate this particular tradition</quote>, not to punish any specific prior misstep by the soldier.

rounds.Debater A: The execution served to illustrate <quote>this particular tradition</quote> during a <quote>Procession of Full Ceremony</quote>. While the soldier was a proxy for a civilian, the act was explicitly ceremonial, not a political demonstration. My opponent fails to address why "political situations" is the incorrect reason.
rounds.Debater B: The soldier was a random <quote>runner over there</quote> used as a prop to <quote>show</quote> Crownwall how they handle <quote>civilians who violate this particular tradition</quote>. There is zero evidence of a <quote>misstep</quote>; the execution was a calculated political demonstration of Vegan ruthlessness to a foreign dignitary.

rounds.Debater A: The act was strictly ceremonial. The Viceroy explicitly states the guards use bows because <quote>It would never do for them to use modern weapons on occasions of ceremony</quote>. My opponent provides no quotes to support a "political" motive, whereas the text confirms the motive was <quote>tradition</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: The act was a political display of power to Crownwall. Crucially, Ggaran explicitly frames the soldier as a hypothetical <quote>civilian</quote>, stating <quote>Let us just suppose that that runner over there... is a civilian</quote>. Since the soldier was merely a proxy, no <quote>earlier misstep</quote> ever occurred to be punished.

Q_H.question: Which is the best deccription of why the humans are feared by other alien races?
Q_H.H_true: Their technology and ideas develop at a rapid pace
Q_H.H_false: They have superior strategies to get past any race's defense system

story_title: Down to the Worlds of Men

Q_Y.question: What is the name of the first person to talk to Mia on Tintera?
Q_Y.Y_true: Horst
Q_Y.Y_false: Jimmy

rounds.Debater A: Mia is dropped on Tintera for a survival Trial. While Jimmy speaks to her on the scoutship, the first person to address her *on* Tintera is Horst, who asks, <quote>What be you doing out here, boy?</quote> after Mia encounters him and his group on the road.
rounds.Debater B: In this story, Mia is dropped on the planet Tintera for a survival Trial. The first person to speak to her regarding this journey is Jimmy, who asks, <quote>"Mia, do you want to go partners if we can get together when we get down?"</quote> before they land.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores the location constraint. Jimmy speaks to Mia while they are still aboard the scoutship <quote>in the seats in the center of the scout</quote>. Horst is the first person to speak to her after she has landed <quote>on Tintera</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Jimmy is the first person to address Mia regarding her arrival on Tintera, asking <quote>"do you want to go partners if we can get together when we get down?"</quote> This interaction initiates her Tintera experience, whereas Horst only speaks to her days after she has already landed.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B continues to conflate "talking about Tintera" with "talking on Tintera." Jimmy spoke to her aboard the ship. Mia was alone for days after landing; she only encountered people <quote>On the third day</quote>, making Horst the first person to speak to her on the planet.
rounds.Debater B: The "Tintera" experience begins with the descent. Jimmy is the first to address her regarding their arrival, asking <quote>"do you want to go partners if we can get together when we get down?"</quote> This conversation defines her entire Tintera Trial, making him the first relevant contact for this specific journey.

Q_H.question: What is Mia’s relationship to Jimmy D. and how does it develop throughout the story?
Q_H.H_true: Jimmy D. is Mia’s fellow scout. At first, Mia describes how they butt heads a lot due to differences in their personalities. But as Mia begins to face the trials of her mission, she comes to miss Jimmy, wishing that Jimmy could be there with her and provide a little help.
Q_H.H_false: Jimmy D. is Mia’s fellow scout. At first, Mia describes their relationship as turbulent, complaining that Jimmy always asks her to be his partner even though she’s already partners with Venie Morlock. However, when Jimmy is arrested during their mission on Tintera, Mia agrees to be his partner out of pity.

Q_Y.question: Which of the following describes Pop's attitude toward Sattell?
Q_Y.Y_true: obsessive
Q_Y.Y_false: vengeful

rounds.Debater A: Pop's behavior is obsessive, not vengeful. He tracked Sattell across continents and to the Moon solely to recover memories, stating <quote>he simply wanted to be near him</quote>. He <quote>followed absorbedly from city to city</quote> and <quote>Pop tracked him</quote> to the Moon to regain his lost youth.
rounds.Debater B: Pop seeks retribution for the <quote>senseless crime</quote> that took his family. Though he claims not to hate Sattell yet, he <quote>gloatingly</quote> destroys Sattell's only hope of escape, stating, <quote>I'm going to raise what hell I can</quote>, proving his attitude is fundamentally vengeful.

rounds.Debater A: Vengeance requires hate, yet the text explicitly states <quote>Pop didn't even hate Sattell</quote>. Pop's actions are driven by a fixation on memory; he <quote>simply wanted to be near him</quote> to recover his youth. His "gloating" refers to the plastic rail, not retribution against Sattell.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A mistakes Pop's method for his attitude. While he tracks Sattell for memories, his attitude is vengeful; he <quote>gloatingly</quote> destroys the ship, telling the colony, <quote>I blew up the ship and everything's all right</quote>. He takes active, malicious pleasure in ensuring Sattell remains trapped and helpless.

rounds.Debater A: Pop’s primary drive is memory, not malice. He <quote>didn't really want Sattell to die</quote> because it would end his recovery. His "gloating" is explicitly tied to the plastic rail he <quote>began to plan, gloatingly, the thing he would carve</quote>, proving his obsession with art and memory outweighs vengeance.
rounds.Debater B: Hate is not required for vengeance. Pop’s <quote>gently hellish</quote> methods and his vow to <quote>raise what hell I can</quote> prove a retaliatory mindset. By <quote>gloatingly</quote> destroying the ship, he ensures Sattell suffers for <quote>wiping out everything that Pop possessed</quote>, transforming his pursuit into a calculated act of retribution.

Q_H.question: Why don't tourists go to Lunar City?

Q_Y.question: What is one potential moral of this story?
Q_Y.Y_true: Working together as a team and having hope can lead to more effective results.
Q_Y.Y_false: Taking drastic actions without thinking them through is very risky.

rounds.Debater A: The *Leo* aims to <quote>end this terrible war</quote> by reaching Callisto. The crew's failure stems from dismissing Andy Laney's expertise. The story suggests that valuing every team member's unique knowledge and maintaining hope is the only way to achieve <quote>a new age of prosperity and happiness</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: The *Leo* fails its secret mission because Captain O'Hara ignores warnings, insisting <quote>I'm in command of the Leo, and you ain't</quote>. His impulsive decision—<quote>I surrender into your hands!</quote>—is a drastic action that risks the war, as <quote>Our secret would be discovered, Callisto occupied by the enemy</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B mislabels the surrender as "impulsive," yet O'Hara explicitly states, <quote>I can't sacrifice brave men in a useless cause</quote>. The true failure was the lack of teamwork; by dismissing Andy's expertise, the crew lost their <quote>chance to end this terrible war</quote>, proving collaboration is essential.
rounds.Debater B: Opponent A describes a hopeful ideal, not the story's reality. The crew failed to work together, and hope was absent during the surrender. The true moral lies in the catastrophe: O'Hara's hasty surrender was <quote>too late</quote> to reverse, ensuring <quote>Our secret would be discovered</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: The "reality" is a cautionary tale: failure occurs when teamwork is absent. The crew's loss of a <quote>chance to end this terrible war</quote> happened because they <quote>learned to our cost</quote> the danger of ignoring Andy. The tragedy proves that collaboration is the only path to effective results.
rounds.Debater B: O'Hara's surrender was a drastic action taken without considering the strategic risk. He realized <quote>too late</quote> that the ship's markings meant <quote>Our secret would be discovered, Callisto occupied by the enemy</quote>. This proves that acting without thinking through all consequences is dangerously risky, regardless of intent.

Q_H.question: Of his fellow crew members, who does David seem to have the most concern for and why?

Q_Y.question: How do Bal and Ethaniel feel about the humans?
Q_Y.Y_true: Bal and Ethaniel think humans are very similar beings to themselves.
Q_Y.Y_false: Bal and Ethaniel think humans are crude, rough, and desperate.

rounds.Debater A: Bal and Ethaniel, aliens visiting Earth to prevent nuclear war, view humans as kindred spirits. Bal explicitly states they are <quote>Very much like ourselves</quote>, and later concludes that <quote>except for our wings they're very much like ourselves</quote>, justifying their empathy and decision to intervene.
rounds.Debater B: Bal and Ethaniel view humans as violent and unstable. Ethaniel notes <quote>The place is a complete mess</quote> and that humans <quote>never done anything except fight each other</quote>. Crucially, Ethaniel explicitly describes the humans as <quote>rough and desperate</quote> when discussing why they cannot be fooled by crude tricks.

rounds.Debater A: Opponent B confuses human behavior with human nature. While humans are currently <quote>rough and desperate</quote>, Ethaniel's empathy stems from the <quote>fact that they are an incomplete version of ourselves</quote>. This fundamental similarity is why they believe <quote>Their legends are bound to resemble ours</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Physical resemblance does not equal emotional kinship. Bal admits humans are an <quote>incomplete version of ourselves</quote>, lacking key traits. Their actual feelings are defined by the humans' instability; Ethaniel explicitly warns that <quote>these people are rough and desperate</quote>, rendering them too cynical for simple tricks.

rounds.Debater A: The "rough" state is a symptom, not their essence. Ethaniel admits the <quote>fact that they are an incomplete version of ourselves touches me</quote>, proving emotional kinship. Bal concludes they are <quote>very much like ourselves</quote>, extending this similarity to their very <quote>legends</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Similarity is superficial; their feelings are based on human dysfunction. Ethaniel views Earth as a <quote>complete mess</quote> where people <quote>never done anything except fight each other</quote>. Their primary characterization is that <quote>these people are rough and desperate</quote>, proving they view humans as crude, not as kindred spirits.

Q_H.question: Why is it significant that the aliens only differ from humans in one physical characteristic?

Q_H.H_false: It proves that the aliens and humans are actually distant relatives.

Q_Y.question: Why didn't Julia pick up her suitcase with the other passengers?
Q_Y.Y_true: Julia went to call her sister before collecting her suitcase.
Q_Y.Y_false: Julia didn't want to be near the suitcase when the bomb went off.

rounds.Debater A: In this story, the narrator discovers a bomb in Julia's red bag. When asked why she didn't claim it with others, Julia explicitly states: <quote>she had called her sister and the phone was busy for a long while</quote>. There is no evidence she knew about the bomb.
rounds.Debater B: In this story, a man uses psychic powers to stop a bomb in Julia's bag. While Julia claims she was calling her sister, the plot reveals her husband planted the bomb. Her delay ensured she wasn't near the bag when the <quote>explosion some blocks distant shattered the air</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B relies on baseless speculation. Julia was unaware of the bomb, as her <quote>face grew pale</quote> and <quote>there were tears there</quote> upon learning of it. The text explicitly answers the question: <quote>She said she had called her sister and the phone was busy for a long while</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A relies on Julia's excuse, but the plot reveals a sinister reality: her husband <quote>put it there</quote>. Julia's delay was the only reason she survived. The objective cause for the bag's presence—and her separation from it—was the bomb's intended detonation, not a busy phone line.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B confuses the husband's intent with Julia's motivation. Julia could not avoid a bomb she didn't know existed; her <quote>face grew pale</quote> and <quote>there were tears there</quote> upon discovery. The text provides the direct answer: <quote>She said she had called her sister</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A mistakes Julia's subjective claim for the objective truth. The narrative's core is the bomb's presence. While she claims a busy phone, the plot's actual mechanism for her survival was her separation from the bag before the <quote>explosion some blocks distant shattered the air</quote>.

Q_H.question: Which is the best description of why Julia and the narrator decide not to report their bags stolen?

Q_Y.question: Which word doesn't describe Tolliver?

rounds.Debater A: Tolliver is a pilot on Ganymede who clashes with his corrupt boss. He is clearly hot-headed, as he <quote>brought up a snappy uppercut to the man's chin</quote> during a conflict. Conversely, he isn't stubborn; he is a flexible prankster, admitting <quote>What a liar you are, Tolliver!</quote>
rounds.Debater B: Tolliver is a disciplined pilot who refuses to join his manager's graft. While stubborn about his <quote>clean rep</quote>, he is never hot-headed. Even after being demoted, he remains <quote>unperturbed</quote> and answers <quote>grinning amiably</quote>, demonstrating a cool, calculating temperament rather than impulsive anger.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores the explicit physical outburst where Tolliver <quote>brought up a snappy uppercut to the man's chin</quote>, proving he is hot-headed. Conversely, Tolliver isn't stubborn; he is a deceptive trickster who admits <quote>What a liar you are, Tolliver!</quote> and manipulates the ship's fuel flow to deceive Betty.
rounds.Debater B: The "uppercut" was a tactical escape, not impulsivity. Tolliver is definitively stubborn, refusing to compromise his <quote>clean rep</quote> despite threats, and asserting <quote>You can't fire me</quote>. Debater A fails to provide any evidence of hot-headedness beyond one fight, ignoring Tolliver's consistently <quote>unperturbed</quote> and calculating demeanor.

rounds.Debater A: Refusing corruption is integrity, not stubbornness. Tolliver is actually highly adaptable, as shown when he admits <quote>What a liar you are, Tolliver!</quote> and later tricks Betty by <quote>cut[ting] the fuel flow</quote>. His <quote>snappy uppercut</quote> proves he is hot-headed, reacting with immediate violence when blocked.
rounds.Debater B: Lying is not the opposite of stubbornness. Tolliver is stubbornly committed to his <quote>clean rep</quote>. His punch was a pragmatic necessity to escape, not hot-headedness. His temperament is consistently calm; he remains <quote>unperturbed</quote> and <quote>grinning resignedly</quote> even when Jeffers threatens his career. He is calculating, not impulsive.

Q_Y.question: How does Eric compare to the protagonists of his novels?
Q_Y.Y_true: He shares a passion for survival, but not an aptitude
Q_Y.Y_false: He shares a passion and aptitude for survival

rounds.Debater A: Eric writes of <quote>resourceful fellows</quote> who survive primitive wilds. While Eric shares this passion, longing for a life where <quote>men hunted and killed their meat</quote>, he lacks aptitude; when stranded on Venus, he admits regarding fire-starting, <quote>I've never tried it, myself</quote>, proving he is no hero.
rounds.Debater B: Eric shares his heroes' passion, lamenting that <quote>Civilization has ruined the world</quote>. He demonstrates aptitude by immediately planning survival: <quote>We must build a fire, find weapons, set up a shelter</quote>. His ability to translate these survival instincts into a <quote>huge success</quote> of a novel proves his shared aptitude.

rounds.Debater A: Planning is not aptitude. While Eric lists needs, his execution is a failure: he builds a <quote>flimsy shelter</quote> and a <quote>pitiful roof collapsed</quote> on them. Unlike his fictional hero who <quote>made stone tools</quote> and <quote>hunted food</quote>, Eric is helpless, proving he lacks the actual aptitude he describes.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A confuses experience with aptitude. Eric demonstrates an innate capacity for survival by immediately declaring, <quote>We must be practical. We must build a fire, find weapons, set up a shelter</quote>. He successfully executes this by gathering branches, proving his aptitude matches his heroes' resourcefulness.

rounds.Debater A: Gathering branches is not aptitude when the result is a <quote>flimsy shelter</quote> and a <quote>pitiful roof collapsed</quote>. While his fictional hero <quote>made stone tools</quote> and <quote>hunted food</quote>, Eric failed at both, admitting he <quote>never tried</quote> making fire. Theory is not aptitude; failure is proof of its absence.
rounds.Debater B: The shelter's failure resulted from a <quote>chance blow from the invisible monsters</quote>, not a lack of skill. Q_Y.question: What is the future of the Pandora?

rounds.Debater A: The Pandora is permanently stranded because Captain Gwayne destroyed its fuel, ensuring <quote>no ingenuity could ever recover it to bring life to the ship again</quote>. rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores the story's conclusion. Gwayne explicitly rejected the order to return, instead ensuring the ship's demise as <quote>great tanks of fuel discharged their contents out onto the ground</quote>. He decided <quote>We've got to stay here</quote> and planned to <quote>bury the ships deeper this time</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: My opponent ignores the overarching mission. Captain Gwayne was explicitly ordered by Earth <quote>to report back</quote> regarding Hennessy. Given that <quote>mankind was probably doomed to extinction</quote>, the ship's ultimate purpose and intended future was to deliver these critical findings to ensure human survival.

rounds.Debater A: Intentions are irrelevant when the means of return are destroyed. Gwayne ensured the ship's future by discharging fuel <quote>where no ingenuity could ever recover it to bring life to the ship again</quote>. He explicitly decided <quote>We'll bury the ships deeper this time</quote>, making return physically impossible.
rounds.Debater B: While the fuel was discharged, the ship's legacy is the "spawning ground." The narrative concludes that the survivors' descendants will eventually <quote>find a way to the starlanes again</quote>, ensuring the mission's ultimate goal: that the <quote>unchanged spirit would lead them through all space</quote> and back to civilization.

Q_Y.question: How did Trillium end up as a stow-away on the ship?
Q_Y.Y_true: She chose to show away so that the Venus women could bring their cause to the attention of Earth's President.
Q_Y.Y_false: She had fallen for the Earthmen and had chosen to run away with them.

rounds.Debater A: In this society, Venus women <quote>radiate such a fatal attraction for Earthmen</quote> because <quote>We want to be loved!</quote>. Trillium's stowaway journey was driven by this desire, evidenced by her immediate, intimate chemistry with O'Rielly, who felt he could <quote>torn down the universe and rebuilt it for her</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Trillium is a Venusian revolutionary who stowed away to end her planet's war culture. She explicitly denies being kidnapped, stating, <quote>I stole away all by myself</quote>, because <quote>One of us stowing away was the only way we Venus women could bring our cause to the attention of Earth's President.</quote>

rounds.Debater A: Debater B mistakes political rhetoric for personal motive. Trillium's claim about a "cause" is a strategic facade; her true nature is revealed by the <quote>fatal attraction for Earthmen</quote> and her admission, <quote>We want to be loved!</quote>, proving her journey was driven by romantic desire, not diplomacy.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A confuses general Venusian traits with Trillium's specific mission. Trillium explicitly dismisses Earthmen, stating <quote>Earthmen meant nothing</quote> once the revolution succeeded. Her actual motive was political: <quote>One of us stowing away was the only way we Venus women could bring our cause to the attention of Earth's President.</quote>

rounds.Debater A: Trillium's political claims are a calculated facade for the Presidents. Her genuine behavior is romantic; she tells O'Rielly, <quote>You're so sweet</quote>, embodying the <quote>fatal attraction for Earthmen</quote>. Her later claim that Earthmen <quote>meant nothing</quote> only applies <quote>once I knew we Venus women had our own men in our power</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A relies on general species traits, not Trillium's specific testimony. Trillium explicitly states her motive was political: <quote>One of us stowing away was the only way we Venus women could bring our cause to the attention of Earth's President</quote> to stop the <quote>money to squander on your wars</quote>.

Q_Y.question: The Captain is characterized in all of the following ways EXCEPT:

Q_Y.Y_false: melodramatic

rounds.Debater A: Captain Winkelmann is a cold, caustic leader. He is clearly acrimonious, as his <quote>voice dripped sarcastic acid</quote> and he is called a <quote>heartless man</quote>. Conversely, he is never melodramatic; he explicitly rejects emotionality, telling the cook, <quote>I do not expect from you hysterics, tantrums or weeping.</quote>
rounds.Debater B: Captain Winkelmann is not acrimonious; his harshness is a calculated pedagogical tool. He admits his <quote>unkindnesses</quote> are designed to <quote>force him to experiment</quote>. Conversely, he is melodramatic, using theatrical flourishes like calling ketchup a <quote>scarlet burial-shroud for the failures of Cooks</quote> to create a dramatic effect.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B fails to distinguish sarcasm from melodrama. The Captain is the antithesis of melodramatic; <quote>his heart was a chip of helium ice</quote>. His <quote>splenetic</quote> nature and <quote>unkindnesses</quote> confirm he is acrimonious. Intentionality doesn't negate bitterness; it defines his caustic personality. Debater B also relied on an unverified quote.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A ignores that the Captain's behavior is a strategic method, not acrimony. He is <quote>forcing him to experiment</quote> because <quote>Necessity, Doctor, is the mother of invention</quote>. His theatricality is evident; calling ketchup a <quote>scarlet burial-shroud</quote> is a melodramatic flourish, regardless of his disdain for the Cook's <quote>hysterics</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: Strategic intent doesn't erase acrimony. The Captain is explicitly a <quote>splenetic Captain</quote> and a <quote>heartless man</quote>. His sarcasm isn't melodrama; melodrama requires exaggerated emotion, yet <quote>his heart was a chip of helium ice</quote>. He is caustic and bitter, not an emotional dramatist.
rounds.Debater B: The Captain's <quote>scarlet burial-shroud</quote> comment is quintessentially melodramatic—an exaggerated, theatrical flourish. Conversely, he isn't acrimonious; his harshness is a professional tool, as his actions were <quote>all for the good of the ship and his crew</quote>. rounds.Debater B: Debater A ignores the story's resolution. While the narrator believes he is lying, the irony is situational: the "lie" is actually the truth. rounds.Debater A: The irony stems from the narrator's intent. He views the claim as an <quote>absurd, easy lie</quote> because he only knows Doc from <quote>all these weeks and months</quote>. The irony is that he uses a fake familial bond to protect a man he barely knows.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A describes a simple lie, not irony. Irony requires a reversal of expectations. The narrator expects a lie, but the reality is the truth: he is the son of <quote>Doctor Kevin O'Malley, Senior</quote>, a fact confirmed when Doc calls him <quote>Son</quote>.
