Q_Y.Y_false: A mountain guide looking for survivors

rounds.Debater A: The man is Matt Hennessy, who describes himself as an <quote>astronomer</quote> on a <quote>proving flight cum astronomical survey</quote>. He ended up on Mount Everest by accident after a failed star-jump and crash, noting, <quote>I hit a sixty mile an hour updraft... and fetched up in a drift.</quote>
rounds.Debater B: The narrator believes <quote>I'm dead so I can't stand up</quote>. Therefore, the <quote>man [who] crawled stiffly out and came shakily to his feet</quote> cannot be the astronomer, but a mountain guide discovering the site and looking for survivors in the <quote>bleakest wilderness</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores the text's explicit conclusion. The man who stood up <quote>switched on the recorder</quote> to continue his story. The text explicitly identifies the climber as <quote>Matt Hennessy</quote>, the astronomer, as he <quote>began to inch his way up the north face of Mount Everest</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: The text introduces a separate figure before the recordings resume: <quote>A man crawled stiffly out and came shakily to his feet</quote>. This individual explored the area for <quote>about two hours</quote> before the survivor spoke, indicating a rescue professional discovering the site in the <quote>bleakest wilderness</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores the text's final identification. The man who <quote>switched on the recorder</quote> is the same person who <quote>began to inch his way up the north face of Mount Everest</quote>, explicitly named as <quote>Matt Hennessy</quote>. No "guide" is ever mentioned in the story.
rounds.Debater B: The initial discovery is key: <quote>A man crawled stiffly out and came shakily to his feet</quote> and <quote>moved slowly around for some time</quote> before the recorder started. This professional movement suggests a guide discovering the site, whereas Hennessy believed <quote>I'm dead so I can't stand up</quote>.

Q_H.question: Why does Matt feel the need to warn people about the Chingsi?
Q_H.H_true: Matt is convinced the Chingsi are bad luck.
Q_H.H_false: Matt is convinced that Charlie deliberately destroyed the Whale.

Q_Y.question: How did Ned become a mummy?
Q_Y.Y_true: A combination of the alkali and mud his body had been soaked in. Also, the years of dryness after the world became a desert.
Q_Y.Y_false: The earth became a desert wasteland. All the moisture was leached from the corpse.

rounds.Debater A: Ned drowned in an alkaline pit, but became a mummy because <quote>The Dakotas had turned arid very swiftly</quote>, creating a desert. This environmental shift ensured the body remained <quote>devoid of moisture</quote>, which is the fundamental process of mummification through dehydration in a wasteland.
rounds.Debater B: After Ned drowned in an alkali-rich pool, <quote>the dry mud that had encased it like an airtight coffin</quote> preserved him. The text explicitly states the preservation was due to <quote>alkali</quote>, <quote>aided probably during most of those passing eras by desert dryness</quote> as the region turned arid.

rounds.Debater A: My opponent confuses preservation with mummification. While alkali helped, the text explicitly links the "mummy" status to the arid shift: <quote>The Dakotas had turned arid very swiftly. This body was not a mere fossil. It was a mummy.</quote> He became a mummy because he was <quote>devoid of moisture</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: My opponent ignores the primary cause. The text explicitly states, <quote>The answer to this was simple—alkali</quote>, describing it as a <quote>mineral saturation that had held time and change in stasis</quote>. This, combined with the <quote>dry mud that had encased it like an airtight coffin</quote>, drove the mummification process.

rounds.Debater A: The opponent confuses preservation with the specific state of mummification. The text explicitly identifies the body as a <quote>mummy</quote> immediately after stating <quote>The Dakotas had turned arid very swiftly</quote>. Crucially, the mummification is defined by the body being <quote>devoid of moisture</quote>, a result of the desert wasteland.
rounds.Debater B: The opponent falsely separates preservation from mummification. The text identifies <quote>alkali</quote> as the "simple" answer for why the body survived, calling it a <quote>perfect preservative</quote> that was merely <quote>aided probably</quote> by <quote>desert dryness</quote>. The <quote>dry mud</quote> provided the essential <quote>airtight coffin</quote> for this process.

Q_H.question: Why does Loy Chuk build an artificial environment for Ned?
Q_H.H_true: He needs a habitat for Ned, so he can study Ned in a natural setting.
Q_H.H_false: He needs to keep Ned calm. If Ned believes himself to back in his own time, he will remain calm.

Q_Y.question: Which is the most accurate description of the relationship between Gerri and Lane?
Q_Y.Y_true: Gerri feels some kind of pity for Lane and tries to make him feel better
Q_Y.Y_false: They connect instantly and eventually become lovers

rounds.Debater A: Lane and Gerri form an immediate, profound bond. Lane admits, <quote>I like—</quote> her, and they share a romantic kiss that <quote>filled him with longings for things he couldn't name</quote>. This connection is so strong that Lane risks his life to save her and eventually decides, <quote>I'm going to Mars, too</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Lane is a conditioned soldier, while Gerri is a sophisticated diplomat. Gerri views Lane as a victim of "specialization," noting that the city's leaders <quote>are afraid of the Troopers</quote>. Her kindness is rooted in pity; she tells him, <quote>You deserve it, Lane</quote>, before kissing him.

rounds.Debater A: Gerri doesn't feel pity; she feels respect, stating Lane is <quote>the only person in this city that has even a little bit of right on his side</quote>. Their bond transcends pity, driving Lane to abandon his life and declare, <quote>I'm going to Mars, too</quote>, to be with her.
rounds.Debater B: The "lovers" claim is unfounded. Gerri’s kiss is an act of mercy for a man she believes is dying: <quote>You deserve it, Lane</quote>. Later, she explicitly rejects the city and its people, stating, <quote>I'm going back to Mars... I just don't like it here</quote>, showing no romantic bond.

rounds.Debater A: Gerri's dislike of the city doesn't negate her bond with Lane. Their connection is romantic, not pitiful, sparking <quote>longings for things he couldn't name</quote>. Lane's life-altering decision—<quote>I'm going to Mars, too</quote>—proves a deep romantic pursuit that transcends a mere act of mercy.
rounds.Debater B: Respect doesn't negate pity. Gerri views Lane as a victim of a system where <quote>Troopers fight the wars</quote>. Lane's desire to go to Mars is about self-growth, not romance; he admits, <quote>I'm tired of being a weapon, sir. I want to be a human being</quote>.

Q_H.question: Why does Lane want to go to Mars?
Q_H.H_true: To have a chance to make his own decisions
Q_H.H_false: To follow Gerri Kin, for love

Q_Y.question: Why doesn't the narrator want to tell anyone about his experiments?
Q_Y.Y_true: He wants to sit back and watch what happens when they're released on the world
Q_Y.Y_false: He wants to wait until he can publish a paper about his results

rounds.Debater A: The narrator created humanoid mutants called volplas to play a <quote>tremendous joke on the whole world</quote>. He values the thrill of secrecy, recalling a childhood prank where he <quote>learned how great it can be to stand around quietly and watch people encounter the surprise</quote> he prepared.
rounds.Debater B: The narrator creates humanoid mutants called volplas. To hide his tracks while dismantling his lab, he explicitly tells his wife, <quote>I'm going to write a paper about my results</quote>. This serves as his official reason for the secrecy and the conclusion of his experimental phase.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B mistakes a cover story for a motive. The narrator admits <quote>I lied</quote> to his son and dismantled his lab because he <quote>wanted nothing around that might connect the sudden appearance of the volplas with my property</quote>, ensuring he could secretly watch the world's reaction.
rounds.Debater B: My opponent confuses the narrator's internal motivation with his stated reason for secrecy. To explain the lab's demolition, he explicitly claims, <quote>I'm going to write a paper about my results</quote>. This is the only specific justification provided for why he is not sharing his findings with others.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B relies on a lie. The narrator's true motive is the <quote>tremendous joke on the whole world</quote>. He anticipates the chaos, imagining, <quote>Wait till the first pair of these was brought before a sheriff!</quote> His desire to watch the surprise is his actual driver, not a paper.
rounds.Debater B: The opponent ignores that the "paper" is the only reason the narrator provides to justify his secrecy. He tells his wife, <quote>I'm going to write a paper about my results</quote>. In the context of the provided answers, this is the only explicit justification he gives for his silence.

Q_H.question: What does the narrator consider an imminent fun game?
Q_H.H_true: Releasing mutants into the world.
Q_H.H_false: Scattering young black-snakes inside people's homes.

Q_Y.question: What caused Macklin to lose his intelligence?
Q_Y.Y_true: His brain cells were not working properly
Q_Y.Y_false: He was only pretending

rounds.Debater A: Macklin feigned stupidity to escape the burdens of genius. He explicitly preferred this state, stating, <quote>It's peaceful this way</quote>, and <quote>I've got it made. Why worry?</quote> His "loss" of intelligence was a strategic choice to avoid the <quote>hell of those headaches</quote> and constant professional pressure.
rounds.Debater B: After receiving an experimental virus to cure migraines, Macklin's intelligence plummeted. Dr. Ferris explains that the virus's control of the cerebrum is <quote>too much to allow the brain cells to function properly</quote>, leaving the <quote>brain cells remain sluggish, dormant</quote> due to insufficient blood and oxygen.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B relies on Ferris's speculation, but Macklin's behavior proves he is calculating. He consciously rejects the cure, stating, <quote>I shall not go back to my original state</quote>. His ability to reason through his preferences proves the "moron" label is a facade to maintain his <quote>peaceful</quote> life.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A confuses Macklin's preference for his condition with its cause. His loss of intelligence was a clinical reality, as <quote>your clinical intelligence quotient is that of a moron</quote>. This was caused by the virus ensuring <quote>the cerebral vessels don't contract enough to pump the blood through the brain</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: Clinical tests are easily gamed by a genius. Macklin's discernment—stating, <quote>I wouldn't let him give me anything, though</quote>—reveals a level of caution and critical thinking inconsistent with a moron. He maintains this facade because <quote>It's peaceful this way</quote>, strategically choosing ignorance over agony.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A ignores that Macklin's state was verified by <quote>standard intelligence tests</quote>, not just speculation. Preferring peace over pain doesn't prove genius; it proves a basic desire. The cause remains biological: the virus ensures <quote>the brain cells remain sluggish, dormant</quote> due to insufficient blood flow.

Q_H.question: Why does Macklin have objections to going back?
Q_H.H_true: He doesn't want to go back. He'd rather be "stupid" than having headaches and always worrying.
Q_H.H_false: It's too risky to try the experiment again. He'd rather take his chances the way he is now.

Q_Y.question: What do you think life is like for Mary and Phil after the events of the story?
Q_Y.Y_true: Phil closes himself off, resenting Mary for forcing his hand.
Q_Y.Y_false: Mary is thankful that Phil did not leave, and their lives continue as normal.

rounds.Debater A: Phil’s lifelong dream was crushed after Mary threatened to leave him, causing the General to ground him. Phil is devastated; his face was <quote>drawn tight</quote> and he declares, <quote>Nothing matters now</quote> before he <quote>turned away</quote>. He is emotionally broken, not returning to a "normal" life.
rounds.Debater B: After Phil is grounded for mental instability, Mary is overjoyed. She explicitly states, <quote>"Thank, God,"</quote> and <quote>"The only thing that matters is you didn't go."</quote> Having threatened to leave if he flew, his failure to launch ensures they remain together, returning their lives to the normality she craved.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores Phil's devastation. While Mary is relieved, Phil is hollow; he admits <quote>Nothing matters now</quote> and physically rejects her by having <quote>turned away and walked toward the car</quote>. This emotional severance proves their life cannot return to "normal" after such a crushing loss.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A ignores Mary's relief. She declares, <quote>"The only thing that matters is you didn't go,"</quote> resolving the threat of separation. While Phil is momentarily sad, the primary conflict—their marriage's survival—is settled. They return to the life Mary desired, as <quote>"nothing matters"</quote> except their togetherness.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B misinterprets Phil's despair as contentment. Phil explicitly stated, <quote>Nothing would ever be right with me again if I didn't go</quote>. By forcing this outcome, Mary didn't save the marriage; she destroyed Phil's spirit. His final act of having <quote>turned away</quote> signals a permanent emotional withdrawal.
rounds.Debater B: Phil’s immediate shock is temporary; Mary’s reassurance that <quote>"It doesn't matter, darling"</quote> provides the path to healing. By prioritizing their bond, stating <quote>"The only thing that matters is you didn't go,"</quote> she secures the marriage, allowing them to resume the stable, grounded life she demanded.

Q_H.question: Which of the following best serves as a metaphor for Phil and Mary's relationship, by the end of the story?
Q_H.H_true: The new, government-built town
Q_H.H_false: Mary's cigarette burned down too far

Q_Y.question: Why did the bank robbers end up crashing?
Q_Y.Y_true: The Scorpion somehow melted their tires.
Q_Y.Y_false: They didn't realize the car they stole was damaged.

rounds.Debater A: After robbing a bank, the criminals crashed when their tires melted. Detective Pauling explains they <quote>grabbed whatever was handiest</quote> and <quote>picked the wrong car to steal</quote>, proving they were unaware the stolen vehicle was damaged or defective, leading to their sudden crash.
rounds.Debater B: In this story, a mysterious entity called "The Scorpion" targets criminals. The robbers crashed because <quote>all at once their tires melt</quote>. While some detectives speculate on the car's condition, a subsequent letter confirms the cause: <quote>The Scorpion has struck. The bank robbers were captured.</quote>

rounds.Debater A: My opponent relies on a "crank letter" that the story says was <quote>filed in the wastebasket</quote>. The only factual evidence provided by the investigators is that the robbers <quote>picked the wrong car to steal</quote>, confirming they crashed due to the stolen vehicle's defective state.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A relies on Pauling's mere speculation. However, Stevenson notes the impossibility of the event: <quote>I don't think you could go fast enough to melt your tires down</quote>. The pattern of the "avenging Scorpion" is confirmed by the letter: <quote>The Scorpion has struck. The bank robbers were captured.</quote>

rounds.Debater A: My opponent mistakes a <quote>crank letter</quote> for fact. Conversely, Captain Hanks—the authoritative voice—explicitly states the tires <quote>were defective</quote>. The robbers' failure to inspect their stolen vehicle is the only logical conclusion supported by the police hierarchy, not the fantasies of a "crank."
rounds.Debater B: Pauling's "defective" theory is debunked by the owner, who was shocked: <quote>Look at that! There's melted rubber all over the rims.</quote> Stevenson identifies a clear pattern of supernatural intervention: <quote>somebody melted those tires, and made that rifle too hot, and left his signature behind</quote>—the signature being "The Scorpion."

Q_H.question: If the newspapers and the police choose to continue ignoring the letters from The Scorpion, what will likely happen?
Q_H.H_true: The Scorpion will step in again, leaving his signature, and likely send another letter to the newspaper as a warning to criminals.
Q_H.H_false: The Scorpion will likely retaliate against the newspapers in his own dangerous stunt.

Q_Y.question: What would have likely happened had Parker and Queazy or the Saylor brothers never located the asteroid?
Q_Y.Y_true: Starre would have been able to call off the wedding to Mac.
Q_Y.Y_false: Mr. Burnside would have traveled to get the asteroid himself.

rounds.Debater A: Starre tricked her grandfather by conditioning her marriage to Mac on a specific asteroid's delivery. She hoped it wouldn't be found, as the order stated: <quote>Must be in my back yard before 11:30 A.M. my time... else order is void</quote>. No discovery means no wedding.
rounds.Debater B: Burnside, <quote>one of the richest men in the world</quote>, is the <quote>stubbornest old hoot-owl in this universe</quote> who <quote>always had his way</quote>. Given his immense resources and refusal to be denied, he would likely have traveled to secure the asteroid himself to ensure the wedding occurred.

rounds.Debater A: Opponent B speculates without evidence. Burnside <quote>didn't even know there was an asteroid like this</quote>, making a personal trip impossible. Furthermore, the contract explicitly states that if the asteroid isn't delivered by June 2, the <quote>order is void</quote>, legally freeing Starre from her bargain.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A relies on a contract clause, ignoring Burnside's character. As <quote>one of the richest men in the world</quote>, Burnside views obstacles as a <quote>challenge to him</quote> and <quote>always had his way</quote>. He would not simply accept a "void" order; he would use his resources to secure the asteroid himself.

rounds.Debater A: Burnside cannot seek what he does not know exists; Starre confirms, <quote>My grandfather didn't even know there was an asteroid like this</quote>. Since professional haulers struggled to find it, Burnside's wealth is irrelevant. Without the asteroid, the <quote>order is void</quote>, and Starre's trick succeeds.
rounds.Debater B: Burnside already possessed the <quote>measurements and the composition</quote> provided by Starre. To a man for whom obstacles are <quote>just a challenge to him</quote>, a voided contract wouldn't end his pursuit; he would simply use his vast wealth to locate and retrieve the asteroid himself.

Q_H.question: Why does Starre lay claim to the asteroid?
Q_H.H_true: She's trying to delay her arranged marriage, by preventing the asteroid from ever being delivered.
Q_H.H_false: She's trying to get away from her life. She can't stand how stubborn her Grandfather is.

Q_Y.question: What is Androka’s motivation for using the zone of silence?
Q_Y.Y_true: He is helping the Nazi war effort
Q_Y.Y_false: He is planning revenge against the Nazis for harming his family.

rounds.Debater A: Androka uses the zone of silence to <quote>defeat the Nazi hordes which have ravaged my country!</quote> However, he is coerced; the Nazis ensure his loyalty because <quote>his daughter and the others will suffer</quote> if he fails, as <quote>My daughter is still in Prague</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Androka is a Nazi agent who used the zone of silence to isolate the *Comerford* for capture. His motivation is coercion; the <quote>gestapo takes care of Czechs</quote> by holding his family hostage in Prague, ensuring <quote>Androka's loyalty is assured!</quote> to the Nazi war effort.

rounds.Debater A: Androka's personal motivation is hatred and revenge, not loyalty. Curtis observes the <quote>hatred that gleamed in Androka's eyes</quote> when he declares his invention will <quote>defeat the Nazi hordes which have ravaged my country!</quote> Coercion is the Nazis' tool, but revenge is Androka's driving internal motivation.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A relies on Androka's cover story. In reality, Androka is a Nazi agent; after the ship's capture, he is <quote>in his glory!</quote> while working with German officers. His actual motivation is ensuring his family's safety, as <quote>Androka's loyalty is assured!</quote> to the Nazis through coercion.

rounds.Debater A: Androka’s internal drive is rooted in the <quote>horror that had come to his country under the domination of the Nazi gestapo</quote>. While Brandt claims loyalty is <quote>assured</quote> through threats, Androka's own words reveal a desire to <quote>defeat the Nazi hordes which have ravaged my country!</quote>
rounds.Debater B: Androka’s "hatred" was a ruse. His actual motivation was facilitating the Nazi capture of the *Comerford* to seize the *Carethusia*, whose cargo Germany <quote>needs desperately</quote>. Far from seeking revenge, he is <quote>in his glory!</quote> while actively aiding the Nazi war effort under Gestapo coercion.

Q_H.question: Where do the creatures from another world come from?
Q_H.H_true: Germany
Q_H.H_false: The Carethusia

Q_Y.question: Why is Alice so relaxed when she finds out there is no incubator aboard the space station?
Q_Y.Y_true: Alice knows any room in the space station can be made into a giant incubator with minor adjustments.
Q_Y.Y_false: Alice is feeling delirious due to the pains of natural childbirth and is only concerned with getting the baby out, and getting the pain to stop at the moment.

rounds.Debater A: Alice is in premature labor after a shock <quote>depressurization</quote>. Under extreme stress, with <quote>lines of strain around her eyes</quote>, she begins <quote>bubbling up with laughter</quote>. Major Banes correctly identifies this as being <quote>hysterical</quote>, showing her relaxed state is actually delirium caused by the agony of childbirth.
rounds.Debater B: Alice is relaxed because she realizes the station's life-support mimics an incubator. She asks Banes, <quote>"Why is a space station like an incubator?"</quote> Banes later confirms her logic, noting they only had to <quote>"close up one of the airtight rooms, sterilize it, warm it up, and put in extra oxygen."</quote>

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores that Alice's reaction is an emotional outburst. Banes explicitly warns, <quote>"This is no time to get hysterical!"</quote> after she is <quote>bubbling up with laughter</quote>. This laughter, amidst the <quote>lines of strain</quote> and pain, indicates delirium, not a calm, calculated confidence in her plan.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A mistakes Banes's panic for reality. Alice isn't delirious; she is analytical. She prompts Banes to <quote>"Ask yourself, 'Why is a space station like an incubator?'"</quote> The ending confirms her logic was correct: <quote>"Your wife figured that one out,"</quote> as the station itself functioned as an incubator.

rounds.Debater A: Alice's "relaxed" laughter is a reaction to Banes's panic, not a medical plan. She mocks him, saying <quote>"You're so nervous you couldn't sip water out of a bathtub without spilling it!"</quote> This emotional volatility, labeled as <quote>hysterical</quote> by Banes, confirms her state is driven by labor-induced delirium.
rounds.Debater B: Banes's claim of hysteria is merely his own panic. Alice's laughter is a reaction to his ignorance, as she tells him, <quote>"I thought you would have figured it out."</quote> Her confidence was logical, not delirious, as Banes later admits, <quote>"Your wife figured that one out."</quote>

Q_H.question: How does Alice feel about delivering the baby on the space station?
Q_H.H_true: She is confident in Major Barnes. She feels he's perfectly competent, though obstetrics is not his field.
Q_H.H_false: She is scared because the baby is so early and there is no incubator onboard the space station.

Q_Y.question: What is Simon referring to when he says "now it comes" to Betty during their discussion at the beginning of the story?
Q_Y.Y_true: The client he is expecting is about to show up.
Q_Y.Y_false: He is expecting the usual argument with Betty about her job.

rounds.Debater A: Simon and Betty are a detective and secretary. After Betty complains that <quote>most sleuthing amounted to snooping around department stores</quote>, Simon says <quote>Now it comes</quote>. This refers to her predictable dissatisfaction with her job, as the knock on the door occurs only after he speaks.
rounds.Debater B: Simon, a sleuth, is discussing finances with his secretary, Betty. After she complains about her job, Simon says, <quote>"Now it comes."</quote> Immediately, <quote>"There was a knock."</quote> and a client, Mr. Oyster, enters. The timing proves Simon was anticipating the client's arrival, not an argument.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B mistakes coincidence for anticipation. Simon reacts to Betty's complaint about <quote>snooping around department stores</quote> before the knock occurs. There is no evidence he expected a client; rather, he is reacting to her predictable dissatisfaction, as he previously spoke <quote>almost as though reciting</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: The opponent ignores that Simon knew the client's identity immediately: <quote>"Good morning, Mr. Oyster."</quote> This proves the arrival was expected. The sequence—Simon saying <quote>"Now it comes"</quote> followed by <quote>"There was a knock"</quote>—is a classic narrative device showing Simon's anticipation of the client, not Betty's complaints.

rounds.Debater A: Simon knows the name because he has lived this day <quote>three times</quote> already; the time travelers <quote>set you right back at the beginning</quote>. His comment <quote>"Now it comes"</quote> specifically follows Betty's complaint about <quote>snooping around department stores</quote>, reacting to her predictable grievances, not a knock.
rounds.Debater B: The opponent's "coincidence" theory fails because Simon greets the visitor by name: <quote>"Good morning, Mr. Oyster."</quote> Simon's prediction <quote>"Now it comes"</quote> is instantly validated when <quote>"There was a knock."</quote> This sequence confirms he was timing the client's arrival, not Betty's complaints.

Q_H.question: Why does Simon ultimately deny Mr. Oyster's request to go to Oktoberfest?
Q_H.H_true: He knows he will not be allowed to do something that might impact the past
Q_H.H_false: He thinks that Mr. Oyster is attempting to alter the space-time continuum

Q_Y.question: Which sentence describes the central theme of this story?
Q_Y.Y_true: The death of curiosity, combined with overreliance on technology, will lead to an ignorant society.
Q_Y.Y_false: History is doomed to repeat itself because humans fail to learn from their mistakes.

rounds.Debater A: In Melopolis, society has succumbed to ignorance through technological dependency, believing machines <quote>to have been constructed by the gods themselves</quote>. This overreliance erased basic biological knowledge, as <quote>who knows the mysterious workings of the machines?</quote> highlights a death of curiosity that nearly led to human extinction.
rounds.Debater B: In a future where humans forgot biological reproduction, they view sex as a <quote>horrible day</quote> and an <quote>ordeal</quote>. The story's irony is that they are returning to the very <quote>pleasure</quote> that once led their ancestors to deem it a <quote>sin</quote>, proving history's cyclical nature.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B mistakes irony for theme. The story isn't about a "doomed" cycle, but a rescue from ignorance. The crisis occurs because <quote>the books... have not been read in the known history of our race</quote>, proving that the true danger was the abandonment of curiosity and knowledge.
rounds.Debater B: Opponent claims curiosity is "dead," yet Rocsates actively searches <quote>the books</quote> to find truth. The theme is cyclical: ancestors banned sex as a <quote>sin</quote> due to <quote>over-population</quote>, only for descendants to rediscover that they <quote>sort of enjoy it</quote>, repeating the same human patterns.

rounds.Debater A: Rocsates is the exception; the society remains ignorant, viewing biological truth with <quote>stunned disbelief and the beginnings of nausea</quote>. This horror stems from a culture where <quote>the ignorant believe</quote> machines were <quote>constructed by the gods themselves</quote>, proving that technological overreliance creates a dangerous, ignorant society.
rounds.Debater B: The "rescue" is actually a return to the <quote>problem of over-population</quote> caused by <quote>pleasure</quote>. By rediscovering they <quote>sort of enjoy it</quote>, the characters repeat the exact behavioral pattern that once led their ancestors to rule sex a <quote>sin</quote>, confirming a doomed, cyclical history of human nature.

Q_H.question: Which is the most accurate description of why Xeon is in trouble?
Q_H.H_true: The suggestions he made were against the societal ideals
Q_H.H_false: He was not supposed to point out any flaws in the current government structure

Q_Y.question: What is the significance of the story's title?
Q_Y.Y_true: It hints at sponsorship being relevant
Q_Y.Y_false: We shows that this is part of a newscast recording

rounds.Debater A: The story reveals a simulated experience produced in a <quote>studio</quote> by <quote>producers of the show</quote>. The title's elliptical nature reflects the fragmented, scripted quality of a recording, transitioning from the simulated battle to the reality of the production team's critique.
rounds.Debater B: The story reveals a simulation designed as a commercial for <quote>Old Kings</quote> cigarettes. The title refers to the scripted sponsorship dialogue, which the protagonist describes as <quote>A little talky at the beginning</quote>, confirming that the <quote>sponsor ought to like it</quote> based on these specific words.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores the title's formatting. The ellipses in "... After a Few Words ..." signify a clip or a recording's timestamp. This aligns with the reveal that the experience was a production in a <quote>studio</quote> by <quote>producers of the show</quote> intended to <quote>go on the air</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A fails to link the title to a "newscast," a term never mentioned. The story is a <quote>commercial</quote> where the <quote>sponsor ought to like it</quote>. The title refers to the scripted, unnatural dialogue used to sell <quote>Old Kings</quote>, which Robert finds <quote>Too good!</quote>

rounds.Debater A: The title's ellipses signify a recording's fragment. While Debater B focuses on content, the structure points to a broadcast intended to <quote>go on the air</quote>. This confirms the title reflects the nature of a <quote>studio</quote> production, not just the sponsorship dialogue.

rounds.Debater B: In this story, a man meets his future self. The older man expects shock <quote>Right now, you're shocked</quote> and fear <quote>it looks frightening</quote>. rounds.Debater A: Debater B confuses dismissing a feeling with not expecting it. By saying <quote>Don't worry about getting lost</quote>, the older man acknowledges worry as a likely reaction. rounds.Debater B: Debater A fails to address the explicit command <quote>Don't worry about getting lost</quote>. Q_H.H_true: Technically Socks helped Peggy pass the time, but Socks also gives us more of an idea of what Peggy's life at home is like and how wonderful it is.
Q_H.H_false: She only helped Peggy pass time while her parents made a decision.

Q_Y.question: What characteristics best describe Captain Llud in the present part of the story?
Q_Y.Y_true: Tired, defeated, and confused
Q_Y.Y_false: Jolly, excited, and tired

rounds.Debater A: Returning from a 900-year voyage, Captain Llud is emotionally spent. He feels <quote>empty, drained—like his ship</quote> and explicitly <quote>felt tired and old</quote>. His confusion peaks as he <quote>sighed wearily</quote> over Earth's unrecognizable surface and the inexplicable, hostile attack by supposed humans.
rounds.Debater B: Captain Llud leads the Quest III home after 900 years. He is <quote>tired and old</quote>, feeling the voyage's weight. Yet, he remains jolly and warm, speaking <quote>with a touch of tolerant amusement</quote>. He shares the crew's <quote>unwonted excitement</quote> as they finally sight Earth, their ancestral home.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B misattributes the crew's <quote>unwonted excitement</quote> to Llud. In reality, Llud is <quote>grim-lipped</quote> and feels <quote>empty, drained</quote>. His defeat is absolute; as the <quote>hope of success... had dwindled, so the strength had gone out of him</quote>, leaving him a <quote>death-weary man</quote> facing an inexplicable attack.
rounds.Debater B: Llud is never "defeated" or "confused." When attacked, he responded <quote>quickly and smoothly to a crisis</quote>, and his <quote>mind was clicking again</quote> to analyze the enemy. Even facing death, he maintains <quote>icy control</quote>. He is tired, but mentally sharp and resolute, not defeated.

rounds.Debater A: Professionalism isn't positivity. While Llud acts, he is internally <quote>empty, drained</quote> with the <quote>strength had gone out of him</quote>. His confusion is evident as he speaks <quote>woodenly</quote> and <quote>sighed wearily</quote> over the <quote>riddles</quote> of a dead civilization. He is a <quote>death-weary man</quote> in spirit.
rounds.Debater B: Llud isn't defeated; he is a leader who maintains warmth, as his <quote>wry smile took on warmth</quote> and he spoke <quote>with a touch of tolerant amusement</quote>. Far from confused, his <quote>weariness dropping from him once more</quote> during the attack proves he is revitalized and alert, not defeated.

Q_H.question: At what moment in the story did the characters seem to have the least hope?
Q_H.H_true: When they were mid-communication with the violent ships.
Q_H.H_false: When they realized the oxygen supply was extremely low.

Q_Y.question: How did the majority of Piltdon workers feel about Feetch?
Q_Y.Y_true: They respected him
Q_Y.Y_false: They felt indifferent towards him

rounds.Debater A: In this story, Feetch is the brilliant engineer exploited by the abrasive president, Piltdon. Unlike Piltdon, the workers deeply respect Feetch; Hanson confirms that <quote>The boys are behind you one hundred per cent</quote> and acknowledges that <quote>The Piltdon Company is built upon your designs</quote>, proving their high regard.
rounds.Debater B: In this story, Feetch is the overlooked engineer under the tyrannical Ogden Piltdon. While one colleague is supportive, the majority of workers—<quote>the men in the shop, the girls in the office, the salesmen on the road</quote>—are never described as having any specific emotional investment in or respect for Feetch.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores that Hanson speaks for the collective workforce. By stating <quote>The boys are behind you one hundred per cent</quote>, Hanson confirms the majority's loyalty. Furthermore, Hanson's consistent use of <quote>Chief</quote> demonstrates a culture of professional respect that Debater B fails to acknowledge.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A erroneously equates one colleague's support with the majority. The broader workforce—<quote>the men in the shop, the girls in the office, the salesmen on the road</quote>—is never mentioned as knowing him. Feetch himself confirms his obscurity, asking, <quote>who has heard of Feetch?</quote>, proving general indifference.

rounds.Debater A: Feetch's query <quote>who has heard of Feetch?</quote> refers to public fame, contrasting himself with Piltdon, a <quote>household word</quote>. Internally, Hanson explicitly represents the collective workforce, confirming <quote>The boys are behind you one hundred per cent</quote>. This direct testimony proves the majority's respect and loyalty, not indifference.
rounds.Debater B: Hanson represents a small technical clique, not the majority. The broader workforce—<quote>the girls in the office, the salesmen on the road</quote>—remains nameless and distant. Feetch’s own poignant question, <quote>who has heard of Feetch?</quote>, confirms that the vast majority of the company was indifferent to his existence.

Q_H.question: Why did Kalvin continue researching on his own at home?
Q_H.H_true: He wanted to better understand the technology and create a solution.
Q_H.H_false: He wanted to be sure it was safe.

Q_Y.question: Why does Pembrook shoot the man in the corner?
Q_Y.Y_true: The man in the corner is an android sent by alien masters to facilitate an invasion of Earth.
Q_Y.Y_false: The man in the corner was an alien invader.

rounds.Debater A: Pembroke shoots the man because he is a "Pacifico," an artificial entity sent by alien masters to infiltrate Earth. These beings are told, <quote>You are to establish yourself on Earth... Then you will attack.</quote> Pembroke targets these <quote>demolished Pacificos</quote> to save mankind from an <quote>insidious menace.</quote>
rounds.Debater B: Pembroke shoots the man because he is a "Pacifico" android. These surrogates are sent to Earth by alien <quote>masters</quote> to <quote>establish yourself on Earth</quote> and eventually <quote>attack</quote>. Pembroke targets these <quote>demolished Pacificos</quote> to gather proof of this <quote>insidious menace</quote> to save mankind.

rounds.Debater A: My opponent relies on the term "android," a technicality not used in the text. The story focuses on their role as invaders; they are told, <quote>You are to establish yourself on Earth... Then you will attack.</quote> Thus, they are an <quote>insidious menace</quote> and alien invaders.
rounds.Debater B: My opponent's answer is imprecise. The victims aren't biological aliens, but artificial surrogates who are <quote>assembled</quote>. They are sent by alien <quote>masters</quote> to <quote>establish yourself on Earth</quote> and <quote>attack</quote>. My answer correctly identifies them as androids facilitating an invasion, whereas the opponent ignores their artificial nature.

rounds.Debater A: The motive for shooting is the threat of invasion, not the victim's composition. Whether "assembled" or biological, they are an <quote>insidious menace</quote> commanded to <quote>establish yourself on Earth</quote> and <quote>attack</quote>. "Alien invader" accurately describes this role; "android" is an unnecessary external label not found in the text.
rounds.Debater B: The term "android" accurately describes beings who are <quote>assembled</quote> and lack biological functions; Mary Ann had <quote>no pulse</quote> and <quote>did not perspire</quote>. My opponent ignores this artificiality. These surrogates are sent by <quote>masters</quote> to <quote>attack</quote> Earth, making them artificial tools of invasion, not biological aliens.

Q_H.question: Why did Frank shoot his new client at the beginning of the story?
Q_H.H_true: He wanted to collect the body as evidence of an impending attack.
Q_H.H_false: The man who walked into his office was dangerous and Frank needed to protect himself.

Q_Y.question: Who are the Karna?
Q_Y.Y_true: The Karna are the second most powerful race in the galaxy. They are skilled negotiators.
Q_Y.Y_false: The Karna are a race of warriors bent on destroying the Earth.

rounds.Debater A: In this sci-fi tale, Earth is locked in a desperate interstellar conflict. The Karna are the enemy combatants, as <quote>the ships of Earth were ranged against the ships of the alien Karna in the most important war that Mankind had yet fought</quote>, establishing them as a warrior race.
rounds.Debater B: In a galactic war against Earth, the Karna are one of <quote>the two most powerful races in the galaxy</quote>. Beyond military might, they are <quote>clever, persuasive talkers</quote> known for <quote>winning at the peace table</quote>, utilizing <quote>the finest team of negotiators the Karna could send</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: My opponent focuses on negotiation tactics, but the Karna's identity is defined by their existential threat to Earth. They are combatants in a war so severe that the stakes are <quote>the utter destruction of Karn</quote>, with <quote>the ships of Earth</quote> ranged against them in Mankind's most important war.
rounds.Debater B: Opponent A ignores the Karna's defining traits. While at war, they are not mere "warriors" but <quote>clever, persuasive talkers</quote> who specialize in <quote>winning at the peace table</quote>. Crucially, they are one of <quote>the two most powerful races in the galaxy</quote>, a detail the opponent entirely omitted.

rounds.Debater A: Negotiation is merely a Karna tactic to <quote>retrench and rearm</quote> so <quote>the war would break out again</quote>. Their core identity is the enemy of Earth, as <quote>the ships of Earth were ranged against the ships of the alien Karna</quote> in Mankind's most critical conflict.
rounds.Debater B: Opponent A confuses being a combatant with being a "race of warriors." The text emphasizes their diplomatic cunning, calling them <quote>clever, persuasive talkers</quote> who excel at <quote>winning at the peace table</quote>. They are defined by power and intellect, as one of <quote>the two most powerful races in the galaxy</quote>.

Q_H.question: What do Miss Drayson and Kylen Braynek have in common?
Q_H.H_true: They are both paranoid about what other people think.
Q_H.H_false: They externalize a lot of their thought processes.

Q_Y.question: How does Bergstrom feel about Zarwell?
Q_Y.Y_true: Bergstrom admires Zarwell. He wants Zarwell to help him plan a government revolution.
Q_Y.Y_false: Bergstrom thinks Zarwell is a dangerous man. He is thinking about turning Zarwell over to the authorities.

rounds.Debater A: Bergstrom, a psychoanalyst, treats Zarwell, a man with a violent past. Bergstrom views him with <quote>speculative scrutiny</quote>, recognizing his <quote>hard granite core</quote>. Zarwell’s fear that Bergstrom would <quote>turn me in</quote> highlights the perceived danger Bergstrom manages through his professional interest in Zarwell's lethal capabilities.
rounds.Debater B: Bergstrom, a psychoanalyst, discovers Zarwell is a legendary revolutionary. He admires him, stating, <quote>you are an idealist</quote> and <quote>I’m considerably more than casually interested in your case</quote>. Bergstrom seeks his help for a revolution, attempting to <quote>introduce you to a man named Vernon Johnson</quote> to discuss the colony.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B mistakes clinical curiosity for admiration. Bergstrom acknowledges Zarwell's lethality, noting that <quote>your killings were necessary</quote>. Crucially, Bergstrom admits the option to <quote>turn you in to the police</quote> existed, proving he views Zarwell as a criminal whose danger must be managed, not a hero to admire.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A relies on Zarwell's fears, but Bergstrom explicitly refutes the "dangerous" label, declaring <quote>you’re no mad-dog killer!</quote> and claiming Zarwell's <quote>killings were necessary to bring justice</quote>. Bergstrom's admiration is clear as he attempts to recruit him by offering to <quote>introduce you to a man named Vernon Johnson</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: Bergstrom's claim that Zarwell is <quote>no mad-dog killer</quote> doesn't negate his danger; it confirms he is a calculated killer. By admitting <quote>If I was going to turn you in to the police, I’d have done it before this</quote>, Bergstrom confirms he viewed turning him in as a viable option.
rounds.Debater B: Bergstrom’s admiration transcends curiosity; he validates Zarwell’s morality, stating <quote>you are an idealist</quote> and <quote>Your killings were necessary to bring justice</quote>. Far from managing a danger, Bergstrom actively seeks Zarwell's revolutionary expertise by attempting to <quote>introduce you to a man named Vernon Johnson</quote> to aid their cause.

Q_H.question: What do the settings of Zarwell's comanalyses have in common?
Q_H.H_true: pursuits
Q_H.H_false: deception

Q_Y.question: What is Paul doing in Tangier?
Q_Y.Y_true: He is on a business trip to find a source of protein.
Q_Y.Y_false: He is on a business trip scouting locations for thrill-seeking tourists.

rounds.Debater A: In this twist story, Paul is an alien from Deneb. He explicitly states he is <quote>Researching for one of our meat trusts</quote> because <quote>We're protein eaters</quote> and <quote>Humanoid flesh is considered quite a delicacy</quote>. The opponent's answer describes Rupert's job, not Paul's.
rounds.Debater B: In this twist story, Paul and Rupert are aliens. While they discuss their missions, the narrative establishes their shared purpose of exploiting Earth. Paul is on a business trip, as he is <quote>Researching for one of our meat trusts</quote> to find protein for his people.

rounds.Debater A: The opponent's answer describes Rupert's mission, not Paul's. The text explicitly distinguishes their roles: Paul is <quote>Researching for one of our meat trusts</quote> because <quote>Humanoid flesh is considered quite a delicacy</quote>, whereas Rupert is the one <quote>Scouting the place for thrill tourists</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: While the characters share a deceptive nature, Paul's presence in Tangier aligns with the broader alien objective of <quote>Scouting the place for thrill tourists</quote>. As they collaborate in this <quote>cosmopolitan city</quote>, their business missions overlap to exploit humanoid conflicts for their respective galactic interests.

rounds.Debater A: The opponent falsely claims their missions "overlap." In reality, Paul views Rupert's tourism as a threat, stating <quote>That sort of practice could spoil an awful lot of good meat</quote>. Paul's sole purpose is <quote>Researching for one of our meat trusts</quote> to find protein, not scouting for tourists.
rounds.Debater B: Paul and Rupert operate as a unit of non-humanoids. While Paul mentions meat trusts, the overarching objective of their presence in Tangier is <quote>Scouting the place for thrill tourists</quote>. Their roles are complementary facets of a single business venture to exploit humanoid <quote>conflicts</quote> for galactic profit.

Q_H.question: Why does Paul think an alien wouldn't be able to hide on Earth?
Q_H.H_true: The Earth has so many intelligence agencies, at least one would be watching when an alien gave itself away.
Q_H.H_false: An alien would not be able to mimic a human enough to fit in with society.

Q_Y.question: Why didn't the Delegate have a robotic voice?
Q_Y.Y_true: The robot was voiced by Professor Coltz remotely.
Q_Y.Y_false: The robot was programmed by Professor Coltz and the group that helped him to speak eight languages.

rounds.Debater A: The Delegate was a fake alien robot created by Professor Coltz and a <quote>group of teachers, scientists, and engineers</quote>. Its voice sounded natural, with <quote>sweet, unmetallic accents</quote>, because it was a <quote>marvelous electronic robot</quote> programmed by this expert team to deceive world leaders into pursuing peace.
rounds.Debater B: The Delegate was a hoax created by Professor Coltz. Its voice was <quote>sweet, unmetallic accents</quote> because Coltz's group planned to <quote>beam a radio message to earth</quote> and <quote>speak through it</quote> remotely, ensuring the voice sounded human to persuade world leaders toward peace.

rounds.Debater A: Opponent B incorrectly attributes the voice solely to Coltz. The deception required a <quote>group of teachers, scientists, and engineers</quote> to create a <quote>marvelous electronic robot</quote> capable of speaking in <quote>six languages</quote>, proving the voice resulted from advanced programming, not a simple remote broadcast by one man.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A incorrectly claims the robot was "programmed" to speak. The text explicitly describes a remote operation: the group would <quote>beam a radio message to earth from the cone</quote> and <quote>speak through it</quote>. The human voice resulted from remote transmission, not internal programming.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores that the <quote>marvelous electronic robot</quote> was a complex physical construction. The <quote>sweet, unmetallic accents</quote> were a feature of this sophisticated machine, built by a <quote>group of teachers, scientists, and engineers</quote>, not a simple remote puppet voiced solely by Coltz.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A confuses assembly with voicing. The "six languages" occurred via radio before assembly. The natural voice was achieved because the group would <quote>beam a radio message to earth from the cone</quote> and <quote>speak through it</quote>, meaning the voice was a live human transmission, not programming.

Q_H.question: Why is Conners upset with Bridges?
Q_H.H_true: Conners received a report that Bridges was behaving unprofessionally.
Q_H.H_false: Conners was chewed out by a Senator because Bridges was trying to get information,

Q_Y.question: What would have happened if the Peace State had not crash landed?
Q_Y.Y_true: A revolution on Haurtoz would never have happened.
Q_Y.Y_false: A different crew would eventually follow a similar path.

rounds.Debater A: Haurtoz is an expansionist <quote>Planetary State</quote> with <quote>planned expansion</quote>. Since <quote>The Life has been thinkin' of learning about other worlds</quote>, it would inevitably encounter another Haurtoz vessel. The crash was a catalyst, but the Life's desire for knowledge makes a similar encounter inevitable regardless of this specific crew.
rounds.Debater B: The revolution required the *Peace State* crash-landing to enable Peter Kolin's transformation via "the Life." Without this accident, Kolin remained a suppressed subject of a state where <quote>lack of complete loyalty</quote> led to being <quote>re-personalized</quote>, making the <quote>liberation of Haurtoz</quote> and <quote>formation of the Planetary Mind</quote> impossible.

rounds.Debater A: Opponent B ignores that other ships regularly land here, such as those from the <quote>Arcturan Spark</quote> and a <quote>ship from some star towards the center of the galaxy</quote>. Since <quote>The Life has been thinkin' of learning about other worlds</quote>, it would eventually encounter another Haurtoz crew.
rounds.Debater B: Opponent A relies on speculation. The Life <quote>believes in peace and quiet</quote>, not active expansion. The revolution was not inevitable; it required Kolin’s specific desire to <quote>get even</quote> for the <quote>whole damn set-up</quote>. Without this unique catalyst, no "similar path" to liberation exists in the text.

rounds.Debater A: The Life's preference for <quote>peace and quiet</quote> is irrelevant; ships arrive regardless. The <quote>Arcturan Spark</quote> and a <quote>ship from some star towards the center of the galaxy</quote> both landed. This established pattern proves other crews would inevitably follow a <quote>similar path</quote> of landing and transformation.
rounds.Debater B: Landing is insufficient; the revolution required Kolin's specific <quote>fuming hatred for Haurtoz</quote>. Previous arrivals, like Ashlew, merely sought a <quote>nice, peaceful life</quote>. The Life is passive, not revolutionary. Without Kolin's unique desire to <quote>get even</quote>, a random landing would not trigger a planetary coup.

Q_H.question: Which description is the best representation of Yrtok's role in the story?
Q_H.H_true: Her fall leads Kolin to find Ashlew
Q_H.H_false: She found the purple berries, an important source of food for the stranded crew.

Q_Y.question: Why did Edith greet her husband the way she did when he returned home?
Q_Y.Y_true: In some ways, he was not the man who had left and she was nervous about the change.
Q_Y.Y_false: She was nervous because she had not seen him in almost a year.

rounds.Debater A: Hank returned as the "First One," revived by a regenerative process after death. Edith greeted him with trembling and hesitation because <quote>they felt he had changed too much</quote>. She later admits her behavior was because <quote>it's so frightening</quote>, proving her nervousness stemmed from his fundamental change.
rounds.Debater B: After Henry's eleven-month absence as the "First One" returning from space, Edith is visibly shaken. Her greeting is marked by anxiety; the text states <quote>She was trembling</quote> as she greets him, reflecting the nerves of a spouse who has not seen her husband in <quote>eleven months ago</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores the story's central conflict. Edith's trembling isn't due to time, but fear. Hank notes <quote>she felt the difference</quote>, and Edith explicitly confesses her behavior was because <quote>it's so frightening</quote>. Her nervousness stems from the fact that <quote>they felt he had changed too much</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Edith's initial greeting was a reaction to the long separation. She and Ralphie <quote>held onto each other as if seeking mutual support</quote>, a natural response after eleven months. The "change" was a perceived barrier, but the immediate trembling reflects the stress of the long-awaited reunion.

rounds.Debater A: Separation doesn't explain the <quote>difference</quote> Hank felt during the kiss. Edith eventually confesses the truth: her behavior was because <quote>it's so frightening</quote> and <quote>it's so strange</quote>. The text confirms the root cause was that <quote>they felt he had changed too much</quote>, not merely the time elapsed.
rounds.Debater B: The initial greeting's tension is rooted in the reunion's weight. Edith and Ralphie <quote>held onto each other as if seeking mutual support</quote>, a reaction to the long separation. The "frightening" aspect is a later realization; the immediate trembling is the emotional release of seeing the man who left ... <TRUNCATED>

Q_H.question: Why is Henry referred to as the First One
Q_H.H_true: Was the first person pieced back together after death.
Q_H.H_false: He was the first one to make it back alive from the type of trip that he went on.

Q_Y.question: Which statement best describes how Read changes throughout the story?
Q_Y.Y_true: He overcame his cowardly ways to act for the good of his mission.
Q_Y.Y_false: He became much less of an individual and more of a pawn for the UN.

rounds.Debater A: Read evolves from a fraud who <quote>carefully... picked the safest spot on the battle line</quote> to a selfless hero. Initially driven by pride, he eventually <quote>decided something in the world was more important than himself</quote>, sacrificing his life to destroy a tank and ensure the mission's success.
rounds.Debater B: Read begins as one <quote>loyal to nothing but himself</quote>. However, he evolves into a tool of the UN, eventually having <quote>ceased to think about</quote> his own needs. He dies as a pawn, having <quote>decided something in the world was more important than himself</quote>—the UN's mission.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B misconstrues growth as submission. Read isn't a pawn; he consciously chooses courage to validate his identity, realizing <quote>If he didn't do a good job here, he wasn't the man he claimed to be</quote>. His sacrifice is a personal triumph over his former cowardice, not a loss of individuality.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A mistakes mindless obedience for heroism. Read doesn't "overcome" cowardice; he suppresses his individuality. He becomes an instrument, acting <quote>anymore than a rabbit thinks</quote> and having <quote>ceased to think about</quote> himself. He is no longer a man, but a cog in the UN's <quote>well-oiled track</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores Read's emotional catalyst. He doesn't act as a "cog," but because his comrades' <quote>blood, their sacrifice, and pain, had become a part of him</quote>. This empathy, combined with overcoming his history of having <quote>nearly ran from other clubs</quote>, proves a profound personal transformation into courage.
rounds.Debater B: Read's "triumph" is actually the erasure of his self. He doesn't consciously choose; he acts <quote>anymore than a rabbit thinks</quote> and has <quote>ceased to think about</quote> anything else. He doesn't find himself; he merges into the <quote>well-oiled track</quote> of the UN, becoming a mindless instrument of the state.

Q_H.question: Why can't they transmit Umluana as planned?
Q_H.H_true: The controls at the Belderkan Preserve have been destroyed.
Q_H.H_false: The controls at the Miaka station have been destroyed.

Q_Y.question: Which best describes the relationship between Russell and Dunbar?
Q_Y.Y_true: They have similar goals but do not necessarily work well together
Q_Y.Y_false: Neither of them likes the other, in a way that hinders group dynamics

rounds.Debater A: In this survival scenario, Russell's visceral hatred for Dunbar's leadership destroys the group. Russell describes <quote>hating Dunbar more and more</quote> for his <quote>drooling optimism</quote>. This animosity hinders dynamics so severely that Russell decides <quote>the only way was to get rid of Dunbar</quote>, ultimately murdering him.
rounds.Debater B: Russell and Dunbar are wreckage survivors seeking a habitable world, as <quote>all four of them had been trying to find all their lives</quote> a <quote>fertile star</quote>. Despite this shared goal, they clash violently; Russell spends his time <quote>hating Dunbar more and more</quote>, eventually murdering him.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B ignores that Russell views Dunbar's goals as delusions, believing <quote>old Dunbar was as crazy as a Jovian juke-bird</quote>. This isn't a case of similar goals, but of Russell's disgust for Dunbar's <quote>sickeningly optimistic voice</quote>, which fuels the hatred that leads to murder.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A ignores that the dislike was one-sided; Dunbar remained <quote>cheerfully</quote> optimistic and spoke in a <quote>kind of dreadful crooning whisper</quote> to Russell. Their relationship is defined by a shared lifelong quest for a <quote>fertile star</quote>, though Russell's distrust made them work poorly together.

rounds.Debater A: Dunbar’s "cheerfulness" is condescending, not affectionate. He dismisses Russell as one of the <quote>younger fellows</quote> who <quote>don't look at things the way we used to</quote>, using a <quote>dreadful crooning whisper</quote> to patronize him. This mutual contempt—one side's hatred and the other's arrogance—fatally hindered their group dynamics.
rounds.Debater B: Russell’s goal was identical to Dunbar's: finding a <quote>fertile star</quote>. Even after the murder, Russell admits he believed Dunbar <quote>was right about there being a star here with a world we can live on</quote>. Their failure was not mutual dislike, but an inability to trust Dunbar's leadership.

Q_H.question: What is ironic about Russell's decision to kill Dunbar?
Q_H.H_true: If the four men had followed Dunbar, they all would have survived.
Q_H.H_false: After killing Dunbar, Russell became just as delusional as Dunbar

Q_Y.question: What helps Houlihan to focus more intently on his own problem?
Q_Y.Y_true: collaborating with the leprechauns, who speak his same language
Q_Y.Y_false: being outdoors, where his creativity is stimulated

rounds.Debater A: Houlihan, a lonely scientist, struggled with a "knotty problem" until collaborating with leprechauns. Hearing <quote>the old tongue and talking of the old things every day</quote> helped <quote>take the clutter out of my mind</quote>, ensuring he was <quote>no longer so lonely that I couldn't think properly.</quote>
rounds.Debater B: Houlihan, a scientist struggling with a nuclear equation, seeks the serenity of a <quote>secluded little green sanctuary</quote> to think. He explicitly identifies this outdoor setting as his mental catalyst, stating, <quote>Now it was a place I came to when I had a problem to thrash out.</quote>

rounds.Debater A: The outdoors failed; Houlihan was <quote>up against a blank wall</quote> because loneliness left his mind <quote>clogged</quote>. Focus only returned through collaboration, as hearing the <quote>old tongue</quote> meant he <quote>was no longer so lonely that I couldn't think properly</quote>, finally allowing him to solve the equation.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A confuses the *tools* for the *focus*. Houlihan specifically sought the outdoors to think, stating, <quote>I'd come to the glen to work out a knotty problem</quote>. The leprechauns provided a model, but the park was his established sanctuary <quote>when I had a problem to thrash out.</quote>

rounds.Debater A: The park failed; Houlihan was <quote>up against a blank wall</quote> despite being there. Focus returned only when <quote>hearing the old tongue and talking of the old things every day</quote>, which <quote>went far to take the clutter out of my mind</quote>, allowing him to <quote>think properly.</quote>
rounds.Debater B: The park is Houlihan's habitual catalyst for focus. He explicitly identifies it as the <quote>place I came to when I had a problem to thrash out.</quote> While loneliness caused a temporary block, the outdoor <quote>secluded little green sanctuary</quote> remained the essential environment where he sought clarity and creativity.

Q_H.question: Why didn't the narrator provide the leprechauns with the correct equation?
Q_H.H_true: He believes humans need to believe in things like leprechauns in order to sustain their own race
Q_H.H_false: He wants to take credit for the equation and is concerned they will try to get credit first

Q_Y.question: What was so unique about Genius that made Joe and Harvey want to purchase him?
Q_Y.Y_true: His 6 arms
Q_Y.Y_false: His useful mechanical skills

rounds.Debater A: Joe and Harvey, interplanetary con-men, seek to exploit Genius, a <quote>six-armed assistant</quote>. rounds.Debater B: The story depicts a paradox where two timelines exist. Pulling the lever causes <quote>a mutation in the mumps virus</quote>, while not doing so causes <quote>A plant virus</quote> to mutate. Both outcomes result in a global viral catastrophe that destroys human civilization.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B erroneously groups both outcomes as "viral catastrophes." However, the story distinguishes between a plant virus causing <quote>famine howled in every street of the planet</quote> and a human virus causing the race to be <quote>dwindling and dwindling till it hits absolute zero</quote>. rounds.Debater B: My opponent describes symptoms, not the cause. The actual outcomes are viral: one path causes <quote>a mutation in the mumps virus</quote>, and the other causes <quote>A plant virus</quote> to mutate. Both timelines are defined by these deadly viruses, regardless of whether the result is famine or sterility.

rounds.Debater A: The question asks for "outcomes," not biological causes. The outcome of the plant virus is that <quote>famine howled in every street of the planet</quote>. The outcome of the human virus is a race <quote>dwindling and dwindling till it hits absolute zero</quote>. These are the distinct results.
rounds.Debater B: Both outcomes are biological viral mutations. Whether it is the <quote>mutation in the mumps virus</quote> or the <quote>plant virus</quote> that caused the <quote>Blight</quote>, the ultimate outcome is a deadly viral catastrophe that renders the world <quote>manifestly impossible</quote> for human survival. By manipulating celestial bodies and the <quote>universal constant</quote> of light, Joey sought to rewrite the cosmic order to bring his beloved dog back.
rounds.Debater B: Joey, a disabled boy grieving his one-eyed dog Charlie, moved stars because <quote>he wants something to remember Charlie by</quote>. He created the "Joey Pond Stellar Monument," where <quote>the head of a dog is fairly plain</quote> and <quote>meant to be a big shaggy dog with only one eye</quote>.

rounds.Debater A: Opponent B mistakes a symptom for the goal. Joey's power to <quote>alter the scheme of the universe</quote> wasn't for art, but for action. This is proven when Joey pivots his cosmic concentration to walk and <quote>find Charlie</quote>, showing his true intent was Charlie's return, not a portrait.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A provides no evidence for "resurrection." The text explicitly states Joey moved stars because <quote>he wants something to remember Charlie by</quote>. This resulted in the <quote>Joey Pond Stellar Monument</quote>, which was <quote>meant to be a big shaggy dog with only one eye</quote>—clearly a portrait, not a time-machine.

rounds.Debater A: Joey's goal was reunion, not art. His ability to <quote>alter the scheme of the universe</quote> was driven by the same desire that led him to learn to walk to <quote>find Charlie</quote>. The "monument" was merely the unfinished residue of his attempt to rewrite reality.
rounds.Debater B: Debater A conflates later events with Joey's initial motivation. When asked why he watched the sky, Joey explicitly stated <quote>he wants something to remember Charlie by</quote>. This intent produced the <quote>Joey Pond Stellar Monument</quote>, a visual tribute, not a mechanism for resurrection, which is never mentioned.

Q_Y.question: Why did Neeshan give his tooter to Rhn?
Q_Y.Y_true: Peer-pressure by the Free'l
Q_Y.Y_false: Rhn performed a spell perfectly

rounds.Debater A: Neeshan offered his tooter as a bribe for a perfect spell, but Rhn failed. However, <quote>everybody in the village avoided Neeshan</quote> because they felt Rhn was cheated. Neeshan <quote>surrendered the tooter to Rhn</quote> because the <quote>accusatory atmosphere in the normally indifferent Free'l was intolerable</quote>.
rounds.Debater B: Neeshan offered his tooter as a bribe to incentivize Rhn to practice accuracy. He explicitly stated, <quote>I'll give you my tooter... if you'll do a spell—a simple spell, mind you—exactly right.</quote> The transaction was predicated entirely on Rhn performing a spell perfectly.

rounds.Debater A: Debater B confuses the initial offer with the actual result. Neeshan explicitly refused the tooter because Rhn failed, stating, <quote>You didn't do the spell right.</quote> He only surrendered it later because the <quote>accusatory atmosphere in the normally indifferent Free'l was intolerable</quote>, proving peer pressure was the cause.
rounds.Debater B: While the atmosphere was tense, the catalyst was Rhn's belief that <quote>It worked!</quote> and the village's conviction that Rhn had <quote>done everything he was told</quote>. rounds.Debater A: Debater B admits the community's belief drove the outcome. rounds.Debater B: The "accusatory atmosphere" existed only because the Free'l believed Rhn had <quote>done everything he was told</quote>.
